Guide and catalogue

🧭 The Model Database

262 ready-made educational models, from a human heart to a grand piano. Place any of them in any world, then stretch, turn and program it.

Getting there: open Edusim, tap ☰ Menu → Model Database. Search for a word or pick a type, then press Place. The model lands in front of you with an orange 🔨 floating over it. The address is edusim3dweb.com/app.

What you can do with one

  1. Shape it

    Click the 🔨, then Stretch to Shape or Rotate/Move Shape. These are the same handles as the Model Builder. Reset Shape puts it back if you go too far.

  2. Build with it

    Touch it to a cube or to another model, then Connect to Primitive and Render Model. A stretched sphere and a heart can become one object.

  3. Learn from it

    Click the model itself for About this model, then Place an Info Sign to stand its facts beside it. Some models carry a green ▶ starter program. Open it and change a number.

A first project: your own museum

  1. Choose a theme

    Press Clear World for an empty field, or stay where you are. Then search for one topic, such as "Egypt", "space" or "music".

  2. Place three models

    Walk a few steps between each, so each has room to be walked around.

  3. Label them

    Add an info sign to each. Then write one thing the sign does not say, using an activity from the tutorials.

  4. Share it

    Use Save World to download a file that a classmate can open, models and all.

A bigger project: your own village

Build a Village is six activities that use the life-size pieces in the 🏡 Build a Village group: plan where things go, feed everyone, do the fence maths and program a chain of jobs.

For teachers

Every card states the real size and how the model differs from it, because an enlargement that is stated teaches and one that is not misleads. Models simplify, and where one simplifies a lot, such as the Bohr atom, its card says so. Placing a model sends no student data anywhere. A very full world can stutter on an older computer, so the panel shows how full the current world is and warns when it gets there, without stopping anyone.

Every model

Click any model to see it turn slowly, then press Inspect Model to walk around it in Edusim, in a space of its own.

🫀 Human Body 19 models

The pump at the middle of the circulatory system, with its great vessels in place.

  • It has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that push it out.
  • A resting adult heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
  • Red in this model means blood carrying oxygen; blue means blood returning to collect more.

Real size: About the size of a closed fist, roughly 5 inches long. This model: Greatly enlarged.

Try this: Give it a program that changes its size up and down to make it beat.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

The cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem, with the folds that pack a large surface into a small skull.

  • An adult brain weighs about 3 pounds.
  • It contains roughly 86 billion neurons.
  • The folds let far more cortex fit inside the skull than a smooth surface could.

Real size: About 6 inches long. This model: Greatly enlarged.

Try this: Walk round it and find the cerebellum at the back, under the two big halves.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, psychology

A pair of lungs with the windpipe above, one side opened to show the branching airways inside.

  • The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, which leaves room for the heart.
  • Airways branch again and again, ending in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli.
  • Oxygen crosses into the blood through the thin walls of the alveoli.

Real size: Each lung is about 10 inches tall. This model: Greatly enlarged.

Try this: Count the lobes on each side. Why would the two lungs be different?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

A cell with a wedge cut away so you can look in at the nucleus and the organelles around it.

  • A typical animal cell is too small to see without a microscope.
  • The nucleus holds the cell’s DNA.
  • Mitochondria release the energy the rest of the cell runs on.

Real size: Around 10 to 30 micrometres across. This model: Enlarged thousands of times.

Try this: Build a label for each organelle you can name using Create Model and an info sign.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, cells

Two sugar-phosphate backbones twisted round each other, joined by pairs of bases.

  • Adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine.
  • The molecule is only about 2 nanometres wide.
  • The DNA in one human cell would stretch about 6 feet if it were laid out straight.

Real size: About 2 nanometres wide. This model: Enlarged tens of millions of times.

Try this: Program it to rotate slowly so you can follow one strand all the way up.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · biology, genetics, chemistry

A standing adult skeleton on a display stand, built as a teaching model.

  • An adult skeleton has 206 bones. A baby starts with more, and some of them fuse as it grows.
  • The femur, in the thigh, is the longest bone in the body.
  • The smallest bone is the stapes, deep inside the ear.

Real size: About 5 to 6 feet tall. This model: About life size.

Try this: Stand beside it. Which of its bones can you feel in your own body?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, anatomy

An eyeball on a stand with a section cut away to show the lens, retina and optic nerve.

  • Light passes through the cornea and the pupil, and the lens focuses it on the retina.
  • The image on the retina is upside down, and the brain makes sense of it.
  • The retina holds rods, which work in dim light, and cones, which see colour.

Real size: About 1 inch across. This model: Enlarged about 60 times.

Try this: Find the iris, then find the lens right behind it. Which one changes shape to focus? Teacher: The lens changes shape to focus. The iris changes the size of the pupil.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, physics

The outer, middle and inner ear in a cutaway block, from the ear flap to the cochlea.

  • Sound makes the eardrum vibrate, and three tiny bones pass the vibration inward.
  • Those three bones are the smallest in the body.
  • The snail-shaped cochlea turns vibrations into nerve signals, and the loops beside it help you balance.

Real size: The ear canal is about 1 inch long. This model: Greatly enlarged, the inner parts more than the outer ear.

Try this: Trace the path of a sound from the outside world to the cochlea. How many parts does it pass?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, physics

A molar set in the gum and jawbone, cut in half to show the layers inside.

  • Enamel, the outer layer, is the hardest substance in the human body.
  • Under it is dentin, and at the centre is the soft pulp, with nerves and blood vessels.
  • Most adults have 32 teeth, and each root anchors its tooth in the jawbone.

Real size: A molar is under an inch tall. This model: Enlarged about 80 times.

Try this: A cavity starts on the outside. Which layers would it pass through to reach the nerve? Teacher: Enamel, then dentin, then the pulp, where the nerve is.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

A block of skin showing its layers, with a hair follicle, sweat gland and blood vessels.

  • Skin is the largest organ of the human body.
  • Its layers are the epidermis on top, the dermis under it and a fatty layer beneath that.
  • Sweat glands cool you down as their sweat evaporates.

Real size: Skin is a few millimetres thick, and the fat under it can be much thicker. This model: Enlarged many times, with the layers not to scale.

Try this: Find the sweat gland and follow its duct to the surface. Why would that cool you down?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

The whole digestive tract on a stand, from the esophagus to the large intestine, with the liver and pancreas.

  • The small intestine is about 20 feet long, and most nutrients are absorbed there.
  • The liver makes bile, which helps digest fat, and the gallbladder stores it.
  • The large intestine mostly takes back water.

Real size: Fills a person’s abdomen. This model: About one and a half times life size, with the small intestine shortened.

Try this: Start at the top and name each part a bite of food passes through.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

A nerve cell on a long stand, with its branching dendrites, cell body, axon and myelin sheath.

  • Dendrites receive signals, and the long axon carries them away from the cell body.
  • A fatty coating called myelin makes signals travel much faster along the axon.
  • Neurons do not quite touch: signals cross a tiny gap called a synapse.

Real size: The cell body is far too small to see, but an axon can be over 3 feet long. This model: Greatly enlarged, with its axon shortened.

Try this: Follow a signal from a dendrite to the far end of the axon. Where would it go next?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, psychology

A bean-shaped kidney cut in half to show its cortex, pyramids and the ureter that drains it.

  • Most people have two kidneys, each about the size of a fist.
  • Each day your kidneys filter about 150 quarts of fluid from your blood, return almost all of it, and make 1 to 2 quarts of urine.
  • Each kidney holds about a million tiny filters called nephrons.

Real size: About 4 or 5 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 11 times.

Try this: Find the red and blue vessels. Which brings blood in to be cleaned? Teacher: The red artery brings blood in, and the blue vein carries it away.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

An arm on a stand, with the biceps and triceps shown working on the bones of a bent elbow.

  • Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs: one bends a joint and the other straightens it.
  • The biceps bends the elbow, and the triceps straightens it.
  • Tendons join muscle to bone, and the forearm works as a lever.

Real size: About 2 feet long. This model: About two and a half times life size, with some muscles left out so the bones show.

Try this: Bend your own elbow and feel your upper arm. Which muscle got shorter and fatter? Teacher: The biceps, on the front of the upper arm.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, physics

The end of a thigh bone sawn open to show hard compact bone, spongy bone and marrow.

  • Bone is living tissue with its own blood supply, and it can repair itself after a break.
  • Dense compact bone forms the outside, and lighter spongy bone fills the ends.
  • Red marrow inside some bones makes the body’s blood cells.

Real size: A thigh bone is about 18 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 10 times, showing only its upper part.

Try this: Why would a bone be spongy inside instead of solid all the way through? Teacher: Spongy bone is strong for its weight, so the skeleton stays strong without being too heavy to move.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

An artery cut open along its length, with red cells, white cells and platelets flowing inside.

  • Red blood cells carry oxygen, using a protein called hemoglobin.
  • White blood cells help fight infection, and platelets help blood to clot.
  • An artery has thick, muscular walls, since it carries blood under pressure from the heart.

Real size: The largest artery is about an inch wide, and a red blood cell is far too small to see. This model: Greatly enlarged, with the cells much larger than the vessel would really show.

Try this: Find one of each kind of cell. Which is there the most of in real blood? Teacher: Red blood cells, by a very long way.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

A teaching skull on a stand, with its top cap lifted to show the inside and its jaw hinged open.

  • An adult skull is made of 22 bones, not counting the tiny bones of the ear.
  • The lower jaw is the only skull bone that moves freely. Most of the others are locked together at wavy joints called sutures.
  • A baby’s skull has soft gaps between its bones, which let the head pass through birth and the brain grow.

Real size: About 9 inches tall. This model: Enlarged about 5 times.

Try this: Find the sutures on the top. Why might the bones join with wavy edges instead of straight ones? Teacher: The interlocking edges make a stronger joint, like the teeth of a zip.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, anatomy

A full spine on a stand, showing its S-shaped curve, cushioning discs and the spinal cord running through it.

  • An adult spine has 24 separate vertebrae: 7 in the neck, 12 in the chest and 5 in the lower back.
  • Below those are the sacrum and the tailbone, each made of fused bones.
  • Its S-shaped curve and soft discs absorb shock, and the bones protect the spinal cord.

Real size: About 28 inches long. This model: About two and a half times life size.

Try this: Count the neck, chest and lower back vertebrae. Why are the lowest ones the biggest? Teacher: 7, 12 and 5. The lowest carry the most weight.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, human body, health

A knee seen from the front, many times life size and slowly bending, with the kneecap folded down so that the crossed ligaments, menisci and cartilage are all in view.

  • The knee is the largest joint in the human body.
  • Smooth cartilage covers the ends of the bones, and two rubbery wedges called menisci cushion the joint between them.
  • Two ligaments cross inside the knee and stop the shin sliding forward or backward. Cruciate means shaped like a cross.

Real size: About 4 to 5 inches across on an adult. This model: About nine times life size, with the skin and muscle left off, the kneecap folded down out of its place in front of the joint, and a simple hinge in place of the knee’s own roll and glide.

Try this: Find the red and blue ligaments in the middle. Walk round to the side and watch them as the knee bends. What would happen to the shin without them? Teacher: The shin could slide forward and backward under the thigh. The two crossed ligaments hold it in place while the knee bends.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, anatomy, health

🦖 Plants & Animals 32 models

The great Late Cretaceous predator, with its short arms and enormous jaws.

  • It lived about 68 to 66 million years ago, in what is now western North America.
  • It grew to about 40 feet long and stood about 13 feet tall at the hip.
  • Its teeth could be as long as a banana.

Real size: About 40 feet long. This model: Half life size.

Try this: Open Bring it to life and make it turn to watch you as you walk past.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · paleontology, biology, earth history

A plant-eating dinosaur with three horns and a broad bony frill.

  • It lived at the same time and in the same places as Tyrannosaurus rex.
  • Its two brow horns could reach about 3 feet long.
  • It was a herbivore, slicing plants with a beak and rows of shearing teeth.

Real size: About 30 feet long. This model: About 60% of life size.

Try this: Place a T. rex beside it, then use the size notes on both cards to set them to scale.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · paleontology, biology, earth history

A soft-bodied ocean animal with eight arms and a strikingly intelligent eye.

  • An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
  • Most of its neurons are in its arms rather than in its brain.
  • With no bones, it can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak, the only hard part of its body.

Real size: A common octopus spans about 3 feet. This model: About twice life size.

Try this: Look for the shape of its pupil. How is it different from yours?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, marine science

A grey reef shark, darker above and white below, the colouring that hides it from both directions.

  • A shark’s skeleton is cartilage rather than bone.
  • It grows new teeth throughout its life, in rows that move forward to replace lost ones.
  • Being dark above and pale below is called countershading.

Real size: About 6 feet long. This model: A little over life size.

Try this: Its starter program swims it in a circle. Change the numbers to make the circle wider.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, marine science

North America’s best-known butterfly, with its orange wings and black veins.

  • Monarchs from eastern North America can fly up to 3,000 miles to spend the winter in Mexico.
  • Their caterpillars eat only milkweed, which makes them taste bad to birds.
  • The trip back north takes several generations. The monarchs that wintered in Mexico lay eggs in the southern United States, and their young fly on from there.

Real size: A wingspan of about 4 inches. This model: About 16 times life size.

Try this: Open Bring it to life and find a motion that looks like a butterfly.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, life cycles, ecology

A tall garden sunflower, with the spiral seed head that mathematicians love.

  • It is the state flower of Kansas.
  • Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun across the sky. Mature heads settle facing east.
  • The seeds grow in interlocking spirals, and their counts are usually Fibonacci numbers.

Real size: Around 8 feet tall. This model: About one and a half times life size.

Try this: Plant a row of them and stretch each to a different height, like a bar chart.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, plants, mathematics

A worker honey bee, with pollen baskets on its back legs.

  • A worker bee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.
  • Bees tell each other where food is by dancing.
  • A bee has five eyes: two large compound eyes and three small simple ones.

Real size: About half an inch long. This model: Greatly enlarged.

Try this: Program a waggle dance: a straight run, a turn, and back to the start.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, pollination

A northern leopard frog, spotted and crouched ready to jump.

  • A frog starts life as a tadpole with gills and a tail, and changes into an adult.
  • It can breathe through its skin as well as with its lungs.
  • It pushes food down its throat partly by pulling its eyes into its head.

Real size: About 2 to 4 inches long. This model: Greatly enlarged.

Try this: Its starter program makes it hop. How far can you make it jump?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, life cycles, ecology

A box-shaped cell with a corner removed, showing its wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole.

  • A plant cell has a rigid wall outside its membrane, which an animal cell does not.
  • Chloroplasts capture sunlight and make food by photosynthesis.
  • A large central vacuole stores water and helps hold the plant up.

Real size: Around 10 to 100 micrometres across. This model: Enlarged thousands of times.

Try this: Place an Animal Cell beside it. List three things that are different.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, cells, plants

A large flower with part of it opened to show the stamens, the pistil and the ovary.

  • The stamen makes pollen, and the pistil receives it.
  • After pollination, the ovary develops into a fruit holding the seeds.
  • Bright petals attract the insects and birds that carry pollen.

Real size: A few inches across. This model: Enlarged about 12 times.

Try this: Place a Honey Bee beside it. Where would pollen stick to the bee?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, plants, life cycles

A sawn section of an oak trunk, with its bark, sapwood, heartwood and growth rings.

  • In many climates a tree adds one growth ring a year, so counting rings gives its age.
  • A wide ring usually means a good growing year, and a narrow ring a hard one.
  • New wood grows in the thin cambium layer just under the bark.

Real size: A mature oak can be several feet across. This model: About life size.

Try this: Count the rings from the centre to the bark. How old was this tree? Teacher: This trunk has 40 rings, so the tree was 40 years old. The narrow rings mark hard years.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, plants, earth science

An Ice Age relative of the elephant, with long curved tusks and a thick shaggy coat.

  • Large males stood up to about 11 feet tall at the shoulder, and females about 8 feet.
  • The last known population lived on an Arctic island until about 4,000 years ago.
  • Frozen mammoths found in Siberia have kept their hair and skin.

Real size: Up to about 11 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: About 60% of life size.

Try this: Why would a thick coat and small ears both help in the cold?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · paleontology, biology, earth history

A plant-eating Jurassic dinosaur with two rows of tall back plates and four tail spikes.

  • It lived about 150 million years ago, in the Late Jurassic.
  • More time separates Stegosaurus from T. rex than separates T. rex from us.
  • Its four tail spikes were probably used for defence.

Real size: Up to about 30 feet long. This model: About 60% of life size.

Try this: Could this animal and a T. rex ever have met? Compare their cards. Teacher: No. They are separated by about 80 million years.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · paleontology, biology, earth history

A bald eagle perched on a branch with its wings half raised.

  • It has been the national emblem of the United States since 1782.
  • Its wingspan can reach about 7 feet.
  • It is not actually bald: it grows its white head feathers at about five years old.

Real size: About 3 feet tall, with a wingspan up to 7 feet. This model: About life size.

Try this: Compare its beak and talons with your hand. What does each do?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, civics, ecology

The tallest penguin, standing with a chick resting on its feet.

  • Emperors are the tallest penguins, at about 4 feet.
  • The male keeps the egg warm on his feet through about two months of Antarctic winter.
  • They can dive more than 1,500 feet down looking for food.

Real size: About 4 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Stand beside it. Are you taller? Why would big bodies help in the cold?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, geography

A plant in a boggy pot, with its red-lined traps open and one closing on a fly.

  • It is native to just one small area of North and South Carolina.
  • A trap usually closes only when its trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds.
  • It makes its own food from sunlight, and insects give it nutrients its poor soil lacks.

Real size: A trap is about an inch long. This model: Enlarged about 15 times.

Try this: Why might a trap wait for a second touch before it closes? Teacher: It avoids wasting energy closing on a raindrop or a falling leaf.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, plants, ecology

A panda sitting upright and eating bamboo, with the bone that works like an extra thumb.

  • Wild giant pandas live only in the mountain forests of central China.
  • Bamboo makes up almost all of what they eat, and they spend much of each day eating it.
  • A long wrist bone works like a thumb, which helps them grip bamboo stems.

Real size: About 4 to 5 feet long. This model: About life size.

Try this: Why might an animal that eats low-energy food need to eat for so much of the day?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, geography

The largest animal known to have lived, its throat pleats and baleen visible at a quarter of life size.

  • It is the largest animal known ever to have lived, growing to about 100 feet long.
  • It has no teeth: plates of baleen strain tiny krill out of huge mouthfuls of water.
  • It is a mammal, so it breathes air through blowholes and feeds its young on milk.

Real size: Up to about 100 feet long. This model: About 1/4 of life size.

Try this: Pace out its length at this size, then multiply by four. How far is that at school?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, marine science, ecology

A slice through an ant nest, with tunnels and chambers for the queen, the young and the food store.

  • Most ants in a colony are female workers, and the queen lays the eggs.
  • Ants follow chemical trails, called pheromones, left by other ants.
  • Different chambers do different jobs, such as raising young and storing food.

Real size: A nest can be far bigger than this slice. This model: Ants enlarged about 30 times, with the queen and eggs drawn larger still.

Try this: Find the queen. Why would her chamber be deep underground?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology

A wooden hive with its side open and a frame lifted out, showing six-sided cells of honey and young bees.

  • Bees build six-sided cells, a shape that holds a lot of honey for very little wax.
  • Some cells hold honey and pollen, and others hold the eggs and young of the colony.
  • Lorenzo Langstroth patented a hive with removable frames in 1852, and most hives still use the idea.

Real size: A hive box is about 20 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Why would six-sided cells waste less space than round ones? Teacher: Hexagons fit together with no gaps, and round cells leave gaps between them.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, mathematics

Six stages of a bean growing in a slice of soil, from a dry seed to a seedling with true leaves.

  • A seed needs water, warmth and oxygen to start growing. Most do not need light yet.
  • The first root usually comes out before any shoot.
  • The two halves of a bean, called cotyledons, feed the young plant until its leaves can make food.

Real size: The seedling is a few inches tall. This model: Enlarged about 10 times.

Try this: What happens to the cotyledons as the plant grows? Look at each stage in turn. Teacher: They shrink as their stored food is used up, and then they wither.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, plants, life cycles

A large savanna elephant with its huge ears, curved tusks and wrinkled skin.

  • The African savanna elephant is the largest living land animal.
  • Its trunk has no bones and tens of thousands of muscle bundles, and can pick up something as small as a peanut.
  • Its huge ears help it to stay cool by giving off heat from the blood inside them.

Real size: Large males are about 11 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: About 60% of life size.

Try this: Place a Woolly Mammoth beside it. How are their ears different, and why might that be? Teacher: The mammoth’s ears were much smaller, which loses less heat in a cold climate.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, geography

A T4 virus landing on a bacterium, with its faceted head, tail and six long leg fibers.

  • A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria, not people.
  • It lands on a bacterium and injects its DNA through its tail, like a tiny syringe.
  • Phages were discovered in the 1910s, and they are thought to be the most common life-like things on Earth.

Real size: About 200 nanometres tall. This model: Enlarged about 12 million times.

Try this: Why would a virus need a bacterium at all? What can it not do alone? Teacher: A virus cannot copy itself alone. It has to use the machinery of a living cell.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · biology, microbiology, health

The tallest living land animal, with its long neck, blotched coat and short horn-like ossicones.

  • Giraffes are the tallest living land animals, and large males reach about 18 feet.
  • A giraffe has 7 neck bones, the same number as a human, but each is far longer.
  • Its long dark tongue reaches leaves that other animals cannot, even among acacia thorns.

Real size: Up to about 18 feet tall. This model: About 60% of life size.

Try this: Stand beside it. How many of you would it take to reach its head at this scale?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, geography

A large male walking across a slab of sea ice, with its thick pale coat and huge paws.

  • Polar bears are the largest living land carnivores, and they hunt mostly seals from the sea ice.
  • Their hairs look white but are actually clear, and their skin underneath is black.
  • Thick fat and dense fur keep them warm, and their big paws work as paddles and snowshoes.

Real size: Large males are up to about 10 feet long. This model: About 70% of life size.

Try this: Why would losing sea ice be a problem for an animal that hunts on it?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, earth science

Six big cut-open cells in a row, from a cell getting ready to divide to two new ones, with chromosomes lining up and pulling apart.

  • Mitosis is how a cell copies and separates its chromosomes, so it can divide into two new cells with identical chromosomes.
  • Chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell, and spindle fibers pull their copies apart.
  • Your body uses mitosis to grow and to replace old or damaged cells.

Real size: A typical animal cell is about a thousandth of an inch wide. This model: Enlarged about 50,000 times, with only four chromosomes shown so you can follow them.

Try this: Count the chromosomes in each cell. Which stage do you see them lined up in the middle? Teacher: Metaphase. Each new cell ends with four, the same number the first cell began with.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · biology

A slice of leaf as big as a table, cut to show its layers of cells, a vein and the tiny pores on its underside.

  • Leaves use sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen. This is photosynthesis.
  • Most of it happens in tiny green chloroplasts, packed into tall cells near the top of the leaf.
  • Pores called stomata, mostly on the underside, let gases in and out.

Real size: Most leaves are only a few sheets of paper thick. This model: Enlarged about 3,000 to 4,000 times.

Try this: Why are the tall green cells at the top and the loose spongy cells at the bottom? Teacher: The tall cells catch the most light near the top, and the air spaces below let gases move from the stomata.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, plants, chemistry

A rod-shaped bacterium opened along its length to show its loop of DNA and ribosomes, with a long whip-like flagellum behind it.

  • A bacterium is a single cell with no nucleus. Its DNA floats in the cell in a tangled loop.
  • Many bacteria swim by spinning their flagella like tiny propellers.
  • Most bacteria are harmless, and many are useful, including those that help you digest food.

Real size: About 2 millionths of a metre long. This model: Enlarged about a million times, with the flagellum shortened.

Try this: Compare this with the Animal Cell. What does a bacterium not have? Teacher: It has no nucleus and no membrane-wrapped parts such as mitochondria.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, microbiology, health

Five finches on a driftwood perch, each with a differently shaped beak and beside the food it suits.

  • Charles Darwin and his shipmates collected finches like these in the Galapagos Islands in 1835. A bird expert, John Gould, later showed they were closely related.
  • Related species evolved beaks suited to different foods, from big seeds to insects.
  • Peter and Rosemary Grant measured average beak size rising in the very next generation after a drought in 1977.

Real size: About 4 to 6 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 8 times.

Try this: Match each beak to its food. What might happen to the big-beaked finches if only tiny seeds were left? Teacher: Birds whose beaks handle the available food survive and breed more, so over generations the average beak can change.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, evolution, geography

A cluster of mushrooms on a rotting log, cut away to show the white threads that spread through the wood and soil, the real body of the fungus.

  • Fungi are not plants. They cannot make food from sunlight, and feed on living or dead things instead.
  • A mushroom is only the fruiting part. Most of the fungus is a hidden net of threads called mycelium.
  • One honey mushroom in Oregon spreads across about 2,400 acres, and is among the largest living things known.

Real size: A mushroom may be a few inches tall. This model: Enlarged about 8 times, with the spores and threads drawn far larger still.

Try this: Why would a forest fill up with dead leaves and logs if fungi disappeared? Teacher: Fungi are major decomposers. They break dead matter down and return its nutrients to the soil.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology

The five stages of a frog around a pond, from a clump of jelly eggs to a tadpole, a tadpole with legs, a froglet and an adult on a lily pad.

  • Frog eggs have no shell. They are held in a clump of clear jelly that swells in the water.
  • A young tadpole breathes with gills. As it changes, it grows lungs and can breathe air.
  • A tadpole does not drop its tail. Its body absorbs the tail and reuses the material.
  • The change is called metamorphosis, and how long it takes depends on the kind of frog. It can take weeks, or more than a year.

Real size: An egg is smaller than a pea, and an adult frog a few inches long. This model: Every stage made much larger, and not to one scale, so that each can be seen.

Try this: Walk around the pond in order. What is different at each stage, and what has not changed yet? Teacher: The hind legs come first, then the front legs, then the tail shrinks away. The gills give way to lungs along the way.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, life cycles

A block of pond cut open from the bank to the mud, with plants, insects, fish, a turtle and a heron all in their places, and the fish swimming.

  • Producers such as water plants and algae make their own food from sunlight, which is where nearly all the energy in a pond starts.
  • Consumers eat plants or one another. A dragonfly nymph eats tadpoles, a fish eats the nymph, and a heron eats the fish.
  • Decomposers such as bacteria and worms break down dead things in the mud and return their nutrients to the water.
  • Very roughly, only a tenth of the energy at one step of a food chain passes on to the next, which is why there are far fewer herons than insects.

Real size: A pond can be anything from a few yards across to a few acres. This model: A block about 16 feet long, with the animals and plants drawn much larger than they would be and far more crowded together.

Try this: Find three producers and three consumers. Then pick one animal and take it away. What happens to what it eats, and what eats it? Teacher: What it ate tends to increase, and what ate it has less food, so one change spreads through the whole food web.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, ecology, earth science

🪐 Earth & Space 33 models

A cone-shaped volcano with a quarter removed so you can see the plumbing inside.

  • Molten rock is called magma underground and lava once it reaches the surface.
  • A stratovolcano is built from layers of lava and ash from many eruptions.
  • Mount St. Helens, in Washington, is a stratovolcano.

Real size: A real stratovolcano can be well over a mile high. This model: A tiny scale model.

Try this: Find the magma chamber, then trace the path magma takes to the crater.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology

The Earth with a wedge removed, showing the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.

  • The crust is the thinnest layer, from about 3 to 45 miles thick.
  • The outer core is liquid metal, and its motion produces Earth’s magnetic field.
  • The inner core is solid because of the enormous pressure on it, even though it is extremely hot.

Real size: About 7,900 miles across. This model: A tiny scale model.

Try this: Stretch it into a wide oval. Real Earth is very slightly wider at the equator too.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology

A clockwork model of the Sun and all eight planets, each on its own arm.

  • Orreries are named after an Earl of Orrery, who owned one in the early 1700s.
  • Sizes and distances here are not to scale. To scale, the outer planets would be far out of sight.
  • In a real orrery, gears turn the inner planets faster than the outer ones, as in the real Solar System. This model turns as one piece.

Real size: A desktop orrery is usually a couple of feet across. This model: Room-sized.

Try this: Press the green arrow to turn it. Which planets would go faster in the real Solar System?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, history of science

The spacecraft that landed astronauts on the Moon, with its gold foil and four legs.

  • Apollo landed twelve astronauts on the Moon on six missions between 1969 and 1972.
  • It had two stages. The lower one stayed on the Moon and served as the launch pad for the upper one.
  • It flew only in space, so it needed no streamlining at all.

Real size: About 23 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Its starter program lifts off. Add a second object to play the stage left behind.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · space exploration, engineering, history

A six-wheeled science rover with a camera mast and a long robotic arm.

  • NASA’s Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater on Mars in February 2021.
  • It is about 10 feet long and weighs about a ton.
  • A radio signal takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to reach Mars, so rovers are not driven live.

Real size: About 10 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Program a route. Remember, you could not steer it in real time on Mars.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · space exploration, engineering, robotics

The three-stage rocket that sent Apollo astronauts to the Moon.

  • It stood about 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal.
  • It was launched 13 times between 1967 and 1973.
  • Each stage dropped away when its fuel ran out, so the rest had less weight to lift.

Real size: About 363 feet tall. This model: About 1/14 of life size.

Try this: Its starter program lifts off. Can you make it speed up as it climbs?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · space exploration, engineering, history

A rock cracked open to show a hollow lined with purple quartz crystals.

  • Amethyst is a purple variety of quartz, coloured by traces of iron and natural radiation.
  • Many geodes begin as gas bubbles trapped in cooling lava.
  • Crystals grow slowly inward as mineral-rich water seeps through the hollow.

Real size: From fist-sized to taller than a person. This model: A large specimen.

Try this: Stretch it wider and walk up close. How do the crystals change from the rim inward?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology, mineralogy

The ringed planet on a display stand, tilted as it really is, with its banded clouds and ring gaps.

  • Its rings are mostly chunks of water ice, from tiny grains to pieces as big as a house.
  • One year on Saturn lasts about 29 Earth years.
  • Saturn is less dense than water.

Real size: About 75,000 miles across, not counting the rings. This model: A tiny scale model.

Try this: Press the green arrow to spin it. Try stretching it wide, since real Saturn bulges at its equator.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy

The orbiting telescope, with its silver shell, open aperture door and two long solar panels.

  • It was launched in 1990, and astronauts visited it five times to repair and upgrade it.
  • Its main mirror is about 8 feet across.
  • Above the atmosphere, it sees the sky without the blurring that affects telescopes on the ground.

Real size: About 43 feet long. This model: About half life size.

Try this: Why would astronauts need to fix something instead of launching a new one?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, space exploration, engineering

A Voyager spacecraft with its white 12-foot dish, instrument booms and golden record.

  • The two Voyagers were launched in 1977 and flew past the giant planets.
  • Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.
  • Each carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.

Real size: A dish about 12 feet across. This model: Life size, with its two longest booms shortened.

Try this: If you could add one sound to the golden record, what would it be?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, space exploration, history

A block of sedimentary rock with its layers exposed, a river cut and fossils in the cut face.

  • In undisturbed layers, the oldest rock is at the bottom. This is called superposition.
  • Sediment hardens over very long times into rock such as sandstone, shale and limestone.
  • Fossils found in a layer help show how old it is. This block is a teaching example, not one real place.

Real size: Real layers can run for hundreds of miles. This model: A small teaching model.

Try this: Find a fossil low down and one high up. Which animal lived first? Teacher: The lower fossil is older.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology, earth history

A cutaway block where an ocean plate slides under a continent, raising volcanoes and an ocean trench.

  • Earth’s outer shell is broken into plates that move up to about 4 inches a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow, or a little faster.
  • Where an ocean plate sinks under a continent, it is called subduction.
  • Subduction builds volcanic mountains such as the Andes and causes large earthquakes.

Real size: Hundreds of miles across. This model: A tiny scale model, with height exaggerated.

Try this: Follow the sinking plate. Where does the magma for the volcano come from? Teacher: Water driven off the sinking plate makes the mantle above it melt. The model shows this simply, as magma rising from the plate.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology

A landscape in a block, from a mountain and river to the sea, with labelled arrows for each stage.

  • The Sun’s heat evaporates water, mostly from the oceans.
  • Rising water vapour cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain or snow.
  • About 97% of Earth’s water is in the oceans.

Real size: The whole planet. This model: A small teaching model.

Try this: Follow one raindrop from the mountain all the way back to the cloud.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, weather

The orbiting laboratory, with its long truss, huge solar wings and joined modules, on a display mount.

  • It is about as long as a football field, including the end zones.
  • It orbits about 250 miles up and circles the Earth about every 90 minutes.
  • People have lived on it continuously since November 2000.

Real size: About 356 feet across. This model: About 1/10 of life size, with thin parts thickened so they can be seen.

Try this: At one orbit about every 90 minutes, how many sunrises do the crew see in a day? Teacher: About 16.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · space exploration, engineering, astronomy

The first artificial satellite, a polished sphere with four long antennas, on a display stand.

  • The Soviet Union launched it on October 4, 1957, and it was the first artificial satellite.
  • It was a polished sphere about 23 inches across, and it transmitted a simple beep.
  • Its launch started the space race, and NASA was founded the following year.

Real size: A sphere about 23 inches across, with antennas up to about 9 feet long. This model: The sphere is enlarged about 3 times, with its antennas shortened.

Try this: Why would a beep from space have mattered so much to people in 1957?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · space exploration, history

A spiralling storm over a warm sea, with a wedge removed to show the calm eye and the towering eyewall.

  • Hurricanes draw their energy from warm ocean water.
  • The eye at the centre is calm, and the strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.
  • In the Northern Hemisphere, hurricanes spin counterclockwise.

Real size: Often hundreds of miles across. This model: A tiny scale model, with height exaggerated.

Try this: Why would a hurricane weaken once it moves over land? Teacher: It loses the warm ocean water that gives it energy.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, weather

The orbiting infrared telescope, with its gold mirror of 18 hexagons above a huge silver sunshield.

  • It launched on December 25, 2021, and orbits the Sun about a million miles from Earth.
  • Its 21-foot mirror is made of 18 six-sided, gold-coated segments.
  • A sunshield the size of a tennis court keeps it cold, since it sees heat in the form of infrared light.

Real size: The sunshield is about 70 feet long. This model: About 1/3 of life size, with its shield layers spread further apart.

Try this: Count the mirror segments. Why would a mirror this big need to be made of folding parts? Teacher: It had to fold up to fit inside its rocket. There are 18 segments.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, space exploration, engineering

A cutaway hillside with a cave inside, its stalactites and stalagmites meeting in columns.

  • Slightly acidic groundwater slowly dissolves limestone, and that hollows out caves.
  • Stalactites hang down from the ceiling, and stalagmites grow up from the floor.
  • They build up from minerals left behind by dripping water, usually very slowly.

Real size: Some caves run for hundreds of miles. This model: A small teaching model.

Try this: Find a column. How did a stalactite and a stalagmite come to make it? Teacher: They kept growing toward each other until they met.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology

A shuttle orbiter on a display stand with its payload bay doors open and robot arm raised.

  • The shuttles flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011.
  • It launched like a rocket and landed like a glider, so the orbiter could fly again.
  • Thousands of heat-resistant tiles protected it as it came back through the atmosphere.

Real size: About 122 feet long. This model: About 1/5 of life size.

Try this: Why would landing like a glider be different from a capsule falling into the sea?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · space exploration, engineering, history

The Sun with a wedge removed, showing its core and layers, with sunspots on its surface and a looping prominence rising off it.

  • In the Sun’s core, hydrogen fuses into helium and releases enormous energy.
  • That energy takes many thousands of years to work its way out of the Sun.
  • Once it escapes, sunlight reaches Earth in about 8 minutes. The Sun is about 109 Earths wide.

Real size: About 865,000 miles across. This model: A tiny scale model, with its thinnest layer and surface features enlarged.

Try this: Sunspots are cooler than the surface around them. How can you tell from the model? Teacher: They look dark. They still shine, but less brightly than the hotter surface around them.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, physics

A table with the Earth at its centre and eight Moons around it, each half lit by a lamp at one side.

  • Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. The phases come from how much of that half we can see.
  • The cycle from new Moon to new Moon takes about 29.5 days.
  • Phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow. That happens only during a lunar eclipse.

Real size: The Moon is about 239,000 miles from Earth. This model: A small teaching model, not to scale.

Try this: Stand at the Earth and look at each Moon in turn. Which one looks full? Teacher: The one on the far side of the Earth from the lamp.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, earth science

A mountain valley in a block, with a glacier grinding down it, crevasses, moraines and a meltwater lake.

  • A glacier is a huge mass of ice that slowly flows downhill under its own weight.
  • As it moves, it carves valleys into a U shape, and rivers cut a V shape.
  • The rock it carries and leaves behind forms ridges called moraines.

Real size: Many miles long. This model: A small teaching model.

Try this: Find the ridge at the end of the glacier. What does it tell you about where the ice used to reach?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, geology, climate

A heavy weight hung in a frame with a pen resting on a turning paper drum, showing the wiggles of a recorded earthquake.

  • When the ground shakes, the frame moves with it but the heavy weight tends to stay still, so the pen draws the motion.
  • Modern seismographs were developed in Japan in the 1880s by John Milne and others.
  • P waves arrive first and S waves after them, and the gap between them tells scientists how far away the earthquake was.

Real size: An 1880s Gray-Milne seismograph was about 2 feet tall. This model: About 7 feet tall, with its drum turning much faster than a real recorder.

Try this: Find where the P waves and S waves begin on the paper. A longer gap between them means what? Teacher: The earthquake was farther away, because P waves travel faster and get further ahead of S waves.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, physics

A white louvered instrument shelter, a mast with spinning cups and a wind vane, and a rain gauge, standing on a square of grass.

  • The white box with slatted sides is a Stevenson screen. It lets air through and keeps sunlight off the thermometers inside.
  • An anemometer measures wind speed from how quickly its cups spin.
  • A rain gauge measures how deep the rain would be if none of it ran away.

Real size: The mast here is about 10 feet tall. Official stations measure wind higher up, at about 33 feet. This model: Life size.

Try this: Why is the shelter white, and why does it stand up off the ground? Teacher: White reflects sunlight, and being raised keeps it away from heat coming off the ground, so it measures the air.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, math

A block of ground cut away to show the layers of soil from leaf litter to bedrock, with roots, worms and burrows.

  • Soil forms in layers called horizons, from dark topsoil rich in rotted plants down to solid bedrock.
  • It can take hundreds of years or more for an inch of topsoil to form.
  • One teaspoon of healthy soil can hold up to a billion bacteria.

Real size: Usually a few feet deep. This model: A block about 9 feet deep, with the layers drawn thicker than most soils and the small animals enlarged.

Try this: Find the darkest layer. Why is it dark, and why do most of the roots stay in it? Teacher: It is full of humus, the rotted remains of plants and animals, and it holds the most nutrients.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, biology, agriculture

A tall column of ocean from the sunlit surface to a deep trench, its layers darkening downward, with an animal in each zone.

  • Enough sunlight for plant-like plankton to grow reaches only about the top 650 feet of the ocean.
  • Below about 3,300 feet there is no sunlight at all, and many animals make their own light.
  • The deepest known point, the Challenger Deep, is nearly 36,000 feet down.

Real size: Nearly 7 miles deep at its deepest. This model: A column about 18 feet tall, with animals much enlarged, its zones drawn at equal heights for clarity, and the hot vent placed deeper than most real ones.

Try this: Why would an animal in the midnight zone make its own light? Find one and think of two reasons. Teacher: Examples include attracting prey, finding a mate, and hiding from or startling predators.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, biology

Five cut-away blocks in a row showing an animal dying, being buried, turning to stone and finally being exposed and found.

  • Most living things never become fossils, because they rot or are eaten first.
  • Quick burial in mud or sand protects the remains, and over time minerals can replace the hard parts.
  • Fossils are found when moving rock and erosion bring old layers back to the surface.

Real size: Takes thousands to millions of years. This model: Five blocks in a row about 24 feet long, with the fish kept in one pose so you can follow it.

Try this: Which conditions would make a fossil more likely, and which animals are more likely to leave one? Teacher: Fast burial in water and sediment helps, and animals with hard parts such as bones or shells are far more likely to leave one.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, biology

A sphere of pure black inside a glowing, spinning disk of hot gas, with narrow jets shooting from its poles. Based on real images and calculations.

  • A black hole has gravity so strong that past its edge, the event horizon, not even light can escape.
  • In 2019 astronomers released the first image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.
  • The black hole at the centre of our Milky Way, Sagittarius A*, has about 4 million times the mass of our Sun.

Real size: Sagittarius A* is about 15 million miles across. This model: An artist’s view, about 14 feet across and not to scale.

Try this: If nothing escapes a black hole, how can we know one is there? Teacher: From its effects: gas heated until it glows, and stars orbiting something massive that cannot be seen.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, physics

A dark, icy nucleus inside a glowing coma, with a straight blue ion tail and a curved dust tail, both pointing away from the Sun.

  • A comet is a chunk of ice, dust and rock orbiting the Sun.
  • As it nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas and forms a glowing coma and tails.
  • Its tails point away from the Sun, because sunlight and the solar wind push them. Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years, next in 2061.

Real size: The nucleus of Halley’s Comet is about 9 miles long, and tails can stretch millions of miles. This model: A model about 18 feet long, with its tails much shortened.

Try this: The little lamp marks the Sun. Which way would the tails point when the comet is heading away from it? Teacher: Still away from the Sun, so the comet then travels roughly tail first.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy

A glowing Sun, the Moon and the Earth lined up on a long bench, with the Moon’s dark shadow cone touching a spot on the Earth.

  • A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and the Earth.
  • The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away, so the two look nearly the same size in our sky.
  • Only people inside the small dark shadow, the umbra, see a total eclipse.

Real size: The Sun is about 93 million miles away. This model: About 16 feet long, with sizes and distances not to scale.

Try this: Why do we not get a solar eclipse every month, when the Moon goes round the Earth? Teacher: The Moon’s orbit is tilted, so most months its shadow passes above or below the Earth.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, math

The Earth with looping field lines around it, pushed in on the Sun side by the solar wind and stretched into a long tail behind, with auroras at both poles.

  • Earth’s magnetic field is produced by moving molten iron in its outer core.
  • The field deflects most of the solar wind, the stream of particles from the Sun.
  • Some particles are guided toward the poles, where they make the air glow as the aurora.

Real size: On the Sun side the field reaches up to about 40,000 miles into space, and its tail stretches far past the Moon. This model: An Earth about 6 feet wide in a model about 18 feet long, with the field much shortened.

Try this: Why does a compass needle point north, and why are auroras usually seen near the poles? Teacher: The needle lines up with the field. Field lines dip into the Earth near the poles, guiding particles in there.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, physics, astronomy

Two paths from one glowing nebula: an ordinary star that ends as a white dwarf, and a massive star that explodes as a supernova.

  • Stars form when clouds of gas and dust collapse under gravity.
  • A star’s mass decides its fate. In about 5 billion years our Sun will start to swell into a red giant. Later it will shrink into a white dwarf.
  • Massive stars explode as supernovas, leaving a neutron star or a black hole, and scatter new elements into space.

Real size: A star may live for millions or billions of years. This model: A table about 16 feet long, not to scale.

Try this: Follow both paths. Why do scientists say that the iron in your blood came from stars? Teacher: Heavy elements such as iron were made in stars and scattered when stars exploded, and later became part of new stars, planets and people.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, physics

A globe with real coastlines travels around a lamp once a year, its tilted axis always pointing the same way, past markers for the solstices and equinoxes.

  • Earth’s axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and it keeps pointing the same way all year, close to the North Star.
  • Seasons come from that tilt. The half of the planet leaning toward the Sun gets more direct light and longer days.
  • Distance does not cause the seasons. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the north.

Real size: Earth is about 7,900 miles across and about 93 million miles from the Sun. This model: A globe about 2 feet across on a base about 15 feet wide. The Sun and the distance are not to scale, and the orbit is drawn as a circle.

Try this: Stop watching the globe and watch the top of its axis. Which way does it lean when it passes the December marker, and what does that mean for Kansas? Teacher: The axis never changes direction. In December the north leans away from the Sun, so Kansas gets low sunlight and short days.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · earth science, astronomy

⚛️ Chemistry & Physics 29 models

Six protons and six neutrons in the nucleus, with six electrons in two shells.

  • Niels Bohr proposed this kind of model in 1913.
  • It is a simplification: electrons actually occupy fuzzy regions called orbitals, not neat rings.
  • An atom is almost entirely empty space, and to scale the nucleus would be far too small to see here.

Real size: About 0.3 billionths of a metre across. This model: Enlarged tens of billions of times.

Try this: Press the green arrow to spin it. Count two electrons in the inner shell and four in the outer.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, physics

One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms, in the bent shape that makes water so unusual.

  • The two hydrogen atoms sit about 104.5 degrees apart.
  • That bend makes one side of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negative.
  • This polarity is why water dissolves so many substances.

Real size: About 0.3 billionths of a metre across. This model: Enlarged tens of billions of times.

Try this: Place several and arrange the hydrogens of one toward the oxygen of the next.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, biology

Sodium and chloride ions in the repeating cubic pattern that makes every salt grain a tiny cube.

  • Each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions, and each chloride by six sodium ions.
  • Chloride ions are noticeably bigger than sodium ions.
  • The cubic arrangement is why salt grains look like tiny cubes under a magnifier.
  • The rods only show the pattern. In real salt the ions touch, and nothing like a stick joins them.

Real size: Ions are about 0.28 billionths of a metre apart. This model: Enlarged tens of billions of times.

Try this: Find an ion in the middle of the block and count its six nearest neighbours.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry

A row of steel balls hanging on threads, the classic demonstration of momentum.

  • Swing one ball in and one ball swings out the other side. Swing two and two come out.
  • It demonstrates conservation of momentum and of energy.
  • It is named after Isaac Newton, who described the laws of motion, and he did not invent it.

Real size: A desk toy about 7 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 9 times.

Try this: Why do the balls eventually stop? Think about where the energy goes.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics

A classroom microscope with an eyepiece, three objective lenses, a stage and focus knobs.

  • Total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective power.
  • Robert Hooke used one to look at cork and coined the word "cell" in 1665.
  • The focus knobs raise and lower the stage to bring a slide into focus.

Real size: About a foot tall. This model: Enlarged about 7 times.

Try this: A 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies how many times?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, physics, history of science

Three meshed gears of different sizes on a stand, showing how gears trade speed for force.

  • Two gears meshed side by side, like these, turn in opposite directions.
  • A small gear driving a big one turns it more slowly but with more force.
  • The speed ratio is set by the ratio of the numbers of teeth.

Real size: Gears range from wristwatch parts to ship engines. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: Count the teeth on two gears. How many turns of the small one make one of the big one?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, engineering

A lab bench with a beaker, an Erlenmeyer flask, a graduated cylinder, test tubes and a Bunsen burner.

  • A flask’s narrow neck reduces splashing when you swirl it.
  • You read a graduated cylinder at the bottom of the curved surface, called the meniscus.
  • The Bunsen burner was developed in the 1850s and is named after the chemist Robert Bunsen.

Real size: Fits on a lab bench. This model: The glassware is enlarged about 3 times, with the meniscus deepened so it can be seen.

Try this: Which of these would you use to measure a volume exactly? Which to heat a liquid? Teacher: The graduated cylinder measures. The beaker or flask is heated.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, science skills

A battery, a switch and a glowing bulb joined by wires on a board, in one complete loop.

  • Current flows only when there is a complete loop, called a closed circuit.
  • Opening a switch breaks the loop, and the bulb goes out.
  • Alessandro Volta built the first battery in 1800, and the volt is named after him.

Real size: Fits on a desk. This model: Enlarged about 6 times.

Try this: Trace the path from one end of the battery to the other. What would break it?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, engineering

A red and blue bar magnet on a board, with iron filings and small compasses showing its field.

  • Outside a magnet, field lines run from its north pole to its south pole.
  • Opposite poles attract and like poles repel.
  • Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.

Real size: A classroom bar magnet is a few inches long. This model: Enlarged about 10 times.

Try this: Look at the compass needles. Which way would one point right at the north pole? Teacher: Its north tip would point straight away from the magnet's north pole.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics

A triangular glass prism splitting a beam of white light into a band of colours.

  • Isaac Newton used prisms in the 1660s to show that white light is a mix of colours.
  • Glass bends light, which is called refraction. It bends each colour by a different amount, which is called dispersion.
  • Violet light bends the most and red light bends the least.

Real size: A classroom prism is a few inches long. This model: Enlarged about 10 times, with the fan of colours spread far wider than in real glass.

Try this: Name the colours in order from red. Which one has bent furthest from the white beam? Teacher: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Violet has bent furthest.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, history of science

A wooden frame with a block and tackle lifting a heavy weight, its rope running round four wheels.

  • A pulley system is a simple machine: it trades distance for force.
  • With four rope sections holding the load, you pull with about a quarter of the force.
  • To make up for that, you pull about four times as much rope.

Real size: Pulleys range from a clothesline to a shipyard crane. This model: A large demonstration model, with its wheels in one plane so the ropes can be counted.

Try this: Count the rope sections holding the weight. How much easier does that make the lift? Teacher: Four sections hold the weight, so you pull with about a quarter of the force: about 100 pounds for this 400-pound weight, ignoring friction. The fifth run is the one you pull.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, engineering

A freestanding wall of all 118 elements, each a raised tile coloured by its family.

  • There are 118 known elements, arranged in order of atomic number.
  • Elements in the same column often behave in similar ways.
  • Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version in 1869, and left gaps for elements not yet found.

Real size: A classroom chart is a few feet wide. This model: About 16 feet wide.

Try this: Find oxygen and carbon. Which column do the noble gases fill? Teacher: The noble gases fill the far right column, group 18.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, history of science

A long wood and leather refracting telescope on a tripod, of the kind Galileo built.

  • Galileo began building telescopes in 1609, after hearing of the invention.
  • His best ones magnified about 20 to 30 times.
  • In 1610 he reported four moons orbiting Jupiter, evidence that not everything circles the Earth.

Real size: About 3 feet long. This model: Enlarged about 3 times.

Try this: Why was seeing moons around Jupiter such an important discovery?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · astronomy, history of science, physics

A simple motor opened up to show its magnets, its spinning coil, its brushes and its commutator.

  • Current in the coil makes it a magnet, which is pushed and pulled by the fixed magnets around it.
  • The commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the coil keeps spinning the same way.
  • Michael Faraday demonstrated electric motion in 1821.

Real size: A small toy motor is about an inch long. This model: Enlarged many times, with only two poles to keep it simple.

Try this: What would happen if you turned the battery around? Teacher: The current reverses, so the motor spins the other way.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, engineering

A tall coil topped with a metal ring, throwing frozen arcs of artificial lightning.

  • Nikola Tesla invented it around 1891 to experiment with high-voltage electricity and lighting without wires.
  • A few turns of thick wire pass energy to a tall coil of thin wire, which makes a very high voltage.
  • That voltage can break down the air itself, which is what makes the visible sparks.

Real size: From tabletop models to machines many feet tall. This model: A large demonstration model, with its sparks frozen.

Try this: Why would sparks jump from the top ring and not from the bottom?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, history of science

A brass equal-arm balance in perfect level, with a block on one pan and weights on the other.

  • When the pans are level, both sides hold the same mass.
  • It works as a lever, with its pivot at the exact middle of the beam.
  • Balance scales were already in use in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.

Real size: A classroom balance is about a foot wide. This model: Enlarged about 6 times.

Try this: Read the weights on the right. What must the block on the left weigh? Teacher: The weights read 5, 2 and 1 pounds, so the block weighs 8 pounds. It is also how an equation works: both sides are equal.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, mathematics, science skills

A small telescope on a ball mount, with its side opened to show the two mirrors inside.

  • Isaac Newton built his reflecting telescope in 1668.
  • It uses a curved mirror to gather light, which avoids the colour fringes that lenses make.
  • Most large research telescopes today use mirrors too.

Real size: About 6 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 12 times, with its mirror’s curve drawn deeper so it can be seen.

Try this: Follow the light: in through the open end, to the big mirror, to the small one, then where? Teacher: Out through the side of the tube, to the eyepiece.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, astronomy, history of science

Two connected glass cylinders of oil, where a small piston and a light weight lift a much heavier one.

  • Pressure on a trapped liquid spreads through all of it equally. This is Pascal’s principle.
  • A big piston has more area for that pressure to push on, so it lifts with more force.
  • Here the large piston has 16 times the area of the small one, so 1 pound balances 16 pounds.

Real size: From a car jack to a large machine. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: To lift the big piston 1 inch, how far must the small one move? Teacher: About 16 inches. You trade distance for force.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, engineering

Two ball-and-stick models side by side, showing how the same carbon atoms make a gem and a pencil.

  • Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Only the arrangement of the atoms is different.
  • In diamond, every atom bonds to 4 others in a rigid 3D network, which makes it extremely hard.
  • In graphite, atoms form flat sheets of hexagons that slide over one another, so it leaves marks on paper.

Real size: Atoms about 0.15 billionths of a metre apart. This model: Enlarged tens of billions of times, with graphite’s layers drawn closer.

Try this: Pick an atom in each model and count how many others it joins directly. Teacher: Four in diamond and three in graphite.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, earth science

A big polished dome on an insulating column, opened to show the belt inside, with a smaller sphere for making sparks.

  • Robert Van de Graaff developed this machine at Princeton around 1929.
  • A moving rubber belt carries electric charge up the column to the metal dome.
  • Like charges push each other apart, so the charge spreads over the outside of the dome.

Real size: Classroom models are about 2 feet tall, and the biggest open-air one is about 40 feet. This model: About 8 feet tall, with its upper roller shown below the dome so you can see it.

Try this: If you touched the dome, why might your hair stand on end? Teacher: Each hair picks up the same kind of charge, and like charges repel, so the hairs push away from one another.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, electricity

A heavy bob swinging on a long wire over a ring of markers, showing that the Earth itself is turning. It really swings here.

  • In 1851 Leon Foucault hung a pendulum in the Pantheon in Paris to show that the Earth rotates.
  • The swing keeps its direction while the Earth, and the floor with it, turns underneath.
  • At the North Pole the swing would seem to go all the way round in about a day. Farther from the pole it takes longer.

Real size: The one in Paris had a wire about 220 feet long. This model: A much shorter model, about 22 feet tall, with its slow turning sped up so you can see it.

Try this: Time one swing there and back. Would a longer wire swing faster or slower? Teacher: Slower. The time depends on the length of the wire, not on how heavy the bob is.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, astronomy, history of science

A tilted spiral in an open channel with a clear side, turning to carry pockets of water up from a pool to a channel at the top.

  • It is named after the Greek scientist Archimedes, who lived in the 200s BCE, though it may be older.
  • Each turn of the spiral traps a pocket of water and carries it uphill.
  • Screw pumps like this are still used today, including in water treatment plants.

Real size: From a few feet to over 30 feet long. This model: A screw about 14 feet long, in an open channel so you can see inside.

Try this: Why does the water not simply run back down the tube? Watch one pocket as the screw turns. Teacher: Each pocket is held in a low point of the spiral. As the screw turns, that low point moves up the tube, and the water stays in it.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, engineering, history of science

A long wooden ramp with bells set along it, and a ball rolling down faster and faster. Equal spaces of time, growing distances.

  • Galileo rolled balls down ramps to slow falling down enough to measure it.
  • He found that distance grows with the square of the time: after 2 units of time a ball has gone 4 times as far, and after 3 units, 9 times as far.
  • Galileo timed the ball with a water clock. The bells are a later museum idea, spaced so a rolling ball passes one at each equal step of time.

Real size: Galileo’s ramps were several yards long. This model: About 18 feet long.

Try this: Measure the gaps between the bells. What pattern do you see, and what does it tell you about the ball? Teacher: From the ball’s start the gaps grow as 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, the odd numbers, because the ball keeps speeding up.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, math, history of science

A lamp, a card with two narrow slits, and a screen showing the striped pattern they make, with the waves drawn on the bench.

  • Thomas Young showed in the early 1800s that light can behave as a wave.
  • Light from two slits spreads out and overlaps. Where crests meet crests it is bright, and where crests meet troughs it is dark.
  • The result is a row of bright and dark stripes, not just two bright lines.

Real size: A real setup can fit on a table. This model: About 10 feet long, with a red lamp where Young used sunlight, and the waves drawn much larger than real light waves.

Try this: What would you see on the screen if you covered one slit? Teacher: The double-slit stripes would disappear, leaving one broad band of light with only faint bands beside it, because there is no second slit’s light to overlap with.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · physics, light, history of science

Rows of the shapes electrons occupy in atoms: a sphere, three dumbbells and five more complex forms, on a labelled shelf.

  • An orbital is the region around a nucleus where an electron is most likely to be found. It is not a path like a planet’s orbit.
  • Each orbital can hold at most 2 electrons.
  • An s orbital is a sphere, a p orbital is a dumbbell, and most d orbitals have four lobes.

Real size: An atom is about a tenth of a billionth of a metre wide. This model: Enlarged many billions of times, with a slice cut from the sphere so you can see the nucleus.

Try this: Count the shapes in each row. How many electrons can all the p orbitals hold together? All the d orbitals? Teacher: 3 p orbitals hold 6 electrons, and 5 d orbitals hold 10.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, physics

Three clear tanks holding the same particles as a solid, a liquid and a gas, so you can compare how they are arranged.

  • In a solid, particles are held in place and can only vibrate.
  • In a liquid, particles stay close together but can slide past one another.
  • In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely, so a gas fills its whole container.

Real size: Particles far too small to see. This model: Enlarged many millions of times, with the solid spaced out so you can see its bonds.

Try this: Count the particles in each tank. Why does the gas look so different if the count is the same? Teacher: Each tank holds the same number of particles. Only the spacing and arrangement differ, and in a real gas they would be much farther apart.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, physics

A long rack of fifteen test tubes coloured by indicator from pH 0 to pH 14, with everyday things placed beside their pH.

  • The pH scale runs from about 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic.
  • Each step on the scale is a tenfold change in acidity.
  • Lemon juice is about pH 2, pure water is pH 7, and household bleach is about pH 12 or 13.

Real size: A test tube is about 6 inches tall. This model: Enlarged about 5 times.

Try this: How many times more acidic is pH 3 than pH 5? Teacher: 100 times. Two steps of ten is 10 times 10.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, biology

The first true battery: a stack of copper and zinc discs separated by salt-soaked cloth. The small glowing lamp is a modern addition.

  • Alessandro Volta announced his pile in 1800. It was the first battery that gave a steady electric current.
  • Each cell is a disc of copper or silver and a disc of zinc, with cloth soaked in salt water between them.
  • The unit of voltage, the volt, is named after him.

Real size: About a foot or two tall. This model: About 7 feet tall.

Try this: Count the copper and zinc pairs. What would happen to the voltage if you stacked twice as many? Teacher: It would be about twice as high, because the voltage of each pair adds up.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry, physics, history of science

A flask of salty water over a burner, with a long water-cooled condenser dripping pure water into a second flask.

  • Distillation separates a mixture by boiling it and then cooling the vapor back into a liquid.
  • When salt water boils, the water becomes vapor and the salt stays behind.
  • Cold water flowing around the condenser turns the vapor back into liquid.

Real size: About 3 feet long on a lab bench. This model: About 9 feet long.

Try this: Why is the liquid in the second flask clear when the liquid in the first is coloured? Teacher: Only the water boils off. The dissolved salt and dye stay behind in the first flask.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · chemistry

📐 Math & Geometry 17 models

The five regular solids in a row on a shelf: 4, 6, 8, 12 and 20 faces, each in its own colour.

  • There are exactly five solids whose faces are all the same regular polygon, meeting the same way at every corner.
  • For each one, corners minus edges plus faces equals 2. This is Euler’s formula.
  • They are named after the Greek philosopher Plato.

Real size: Any size at all. This model: A large demonstration set.

Try this: Pick one and count its corners, edges and faces. Does Euler’s formula hold? Teacher: Cube: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2. Icosahedron: 12 - 30 + 20 = 2.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

A 3-4-5 right triangle with a square of real tiles built on each of its sides.

  • In a right triangle, the squares on the two short sides add up to the square on the longest side.
  • Here that is 9 tiles plus 16 tiles making 25 tiles, and you can count them.
  • It is named after Pythagoras, though Babylonian mathematicians knew it more than a thousand years earlier.

Real size: Any size at all. This model: One tile is a foot square.

Try this: Count the tiles on each square, then check that 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 5 x 5.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

A chambered nautilus shell cut in half to show its spiral of growing chambers.

  • As it grows, the animal adds a new, larger chamber and seals off the old one.
  • The shell keeps the same shape as it grows, which makes a logarithmic spiral.
  • It is often said to follow the golden ratio, but measured shells usually do not.

Real size: About 8 inches across. This model: Enlarged about 9 times.

Try this: Count the chambers from the centre out. What happens to their size? Teacher: 30 chambers, plus the open body chamber the animal lived in. Each is about 1.1 times as long as the one before.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, biology, geometry

A striped band with one half twist, on a stand, with a surface that has only one side.

  • A Möbius strip has only one side and only one edge.
  • You can make one by giving a strip of paper a half twist and taping the ends.
  • August Möbius described it in 1858, and another mathematician found it the same year.

Real size: Any size at all. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: Make one out of paper, then cut it down the middle. Can you predict what happens? Teacher: It stays in one piece, as a longer loop with two full twists.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

A fractal pyramid made of 256 small pyramids, the same pattern repeated at every size.

  • It is a fractal: each part looks like a smaller copy of the whole.
  • Each step replaces every pyramid with four half-size copies.
  • After four steps, as here, that makes 4 x 4 x 4 x 4 = 256 small pyramids.
