Real size: Any size at all. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: How many small pyramids would the next step make? Teacher: 1,024, which is 256 x 4.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

An upright board where balls have bounced through rows of pegs and piled up in a bell curve.

  • Each ball goes left or right at every peg, as if by a coin toss.
  • Most balls end up near the middle, since there are more paths that lead there.
  • The pile makes a bell curve, which also describes many measurements in nature.

Real size: A desktop model is about a foot tall. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: How many different paths lead to the far left slot? How many to the middle? Teacher: Just one path leads to the far left slot, and the most paths lead to the middle.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, statistics

A wall of coloured bars, each row one whole cut into equal parts, from halves to twelfths.

  • Every row is the same length, because each one is one whole.
  • The bigger the bottom number, the smaller each part is.
  • Parts that line up are equivalent: two quarters reach exactly as far as one half.

Real size: A classroom version is a few feet wide. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: How many twelfths line up with one third? What about with one half? Teacher: Four twelfths equal one third, and six twelfths equal one half.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics

Four cones on a shelf, each sliced at a different angle to reveal a circle, an ellipse, a parabola and a hyperbola.

  • Slicing a cone at different angles gives four different curves.
  • Apollonius of Perga wrote the classic study of them more than 2,000 years ago.
  • Planets orbit in ellipses, and a thrown ball follows very nearly a parabola.

Real size: Any size at all. This model: A large demonstration set.

Try this: Which slice runs exactly parallel to the side of the cone? Teacher: The parabola.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

A table showing the number 1,234 in blocks: a thousand cube, hundred flats, ten rods and single ones.

  • Each place is worth ten of the place to its right.
  • Ten ones make a rod, ten rods make a flat, and ten flats make a cube.
  • This table shows 1,234: 1 thousand, 2 hundreds, 3 tens and 4 ones.

Real size: A classroom thousand cube is about 4 inches wide. This model: Enlarged about 10 times.

Try this: Without counting every little square, how would you check there are 1,234 here? Teacher: Count the groups: 1 cube, 2 flats, 3 rods and 4 ones.

Grades K-2, 3-5 · mathematics

A wooden puzzle of seven stacked discs on three pegs, with a printed rule and a count of the moves.

  • Move all the discs to another peg, one at a time, and never put a bigger disc on a smaller one.
  • Seven discs take at least 127 moves. Each extra disc roughly doubles that, since the minimum is 2 to the power of n, minus 1.
  • The French mathematician Édouard Lucas invented it in 1883.

Real size: A desktop puzzle is about a foot wide. This model: Enlarged about 9 times.

Try this: Work out the fewest moves for three discs, then four. Can you see the pattern? Teacher: Three discs take 7 moves and four take 15. Each is double the last, plus one.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, computer science

A glass-like bottle whose neck passes through its own side and joins its base, with no inside or outside.

  • A Klein bottle is a surface with no inside or outside, described by Felix Klein in 1882.
  • In true form it does not cross itself, but that needs four dimensions.
  • A model in our three dimensions has to pass through itself, as this one does.

Real size: Any size at all. This model: A large demonstration model.

Try this: Compare it with the Möbius Strip. How are they alike? Try tracing a path along the surface. Teacher: Both have only one side, so a path can reach every part of the surface without crossing an edge.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

Seven coloured pieces cut from one square, shown assembled and rearranged into a cat and a boat.

  • The tangram is a Chinese puzzle that spread around the world in the early 1800s.
  • Its seven pieces are 5 triangles, 1 square and 1 parallelogram.
  • However you arrange all seven, the total area stays the same.

Real size: A puzzle that fits in your hand. This model: Enlarged about 10 times.

Try this: What fraction of the whole square is one of the big triangles? What about the small square? Teacher: A big triangle is one quarter. The small square is one eighth.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry, world cultures

A leaning triangle of numbered tiles where each number is the sum of the two above it. The odd numbers are colored, and a familiar shape appears.

  • Each number is the sum of the two directly above it.
  • The numbers in any row add up to a power of 2. Row 1, 3, 3, 1 adds up to 8.
  • Mathematicians in India, Persia and China knew this triangle centuries before Blaise Pascal wrote about it in the 1650s.

Real size: A pattern of numbers with no real size, and it never ends. This model: The first 13 rows, on a sloped stand about 12 feet wide.

Try this: Add up each row. What pattern do you get? Then read down the third slanting line: 1, 3, 6, 10. What comes next? Teacher: The rows add up to 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, doubling each time. The slanting line is the triangular numbers, so 15 comes next.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, history of mathematics

A point travels around a circle of radius 1 while its height draws out a sine wave beside it, so a circle and a wave turn out to be one idea.

  • On a circle of radius 1, the point at any angle sits at (cos, sin) of that angle: cosine is how far across, and sine is how far up.
  • Because the radius is the long side of a right triangle, cos² + sin² = 1 for every angle. That is the Pythagorean theorem.
  • One full turn is 360 degrees, or 2π radians: about 6.28 radius lengths around the edge.

Real size: A circle whose radius is 1 unit, which can be any length. This model: A radius of about 2.5 feet, so 1 unit on the grid is about 2.5 feet. The wave has the same heights, and its length is drawn at half scale.

Try this: At what angles is the height exactly the same as the distance across? Find them on the circle, then find them on the wave. Teacher: At 45 and 225 degrees, where sine and cosine are equal.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, trigonometry

A cone, a sphere and a cylinder of the same width and height, each cut open to show the liquid it holds, beside three tubes that hold exactly the same amounts.

  • A cone, a sphere and a cylinder with the same width and height have volumes in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.
  • In the 200s BCE, Archimedes proved that a sphere holds exactly two thirds of the cylinder around it.
  • He is said to have asked for a sphere and cylinder on his tomb. The Roman writer Cicero reported finding that tomb in Sicily in 75 BCE.

Real size: A rule that holds at any size. This model: Solids about 3 feet across and 3 feet tall.

Try this: If the cone holds 2 cups, how much do the sphere and the cylinder hold? Check the tubes at the back. Teacher: The sphere holds 4 cups and the cylinder holds 6, keeping the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.

Grades 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry, history of mathematics

A wheel with a painted mark rolls one full turn along a ruler marked in its own diameters, and lands just past three.

  • The distance around any circle is about 3.14 times the distance across it. That number is called pi.
  • Pi is the same for every circle, whether it is a coin or a planet.
  • Pi never ends and never repeats. In the 200s BCE, Archimedes showed it lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7.

Real size: A rule that holds at any size. This model: A wheel about 3 feet across on a ruler about 12 feet long.

Try this: Before the wheel finishes its turn, guess where the mark will touch down. How many wheels across is one trip around? Teacher: A little past 3: one turn covers about 3.14 diameters.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, geometry

Eight number wheels showing only 0 and 1 count upward by themselves, each one tipping the next as it rolls over, with the same number in ordinary digits beside them.

  • Computers store everything as 0s and 1s, called bits, because a tiny switch is either off or on.
  • Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.
  • Eight bits make one byte, which can count from 0 up to 255.

Real size: A computer chip holds billions of far smaller switches. This model: A desk-sized counter about 10 feet wide. Real computers do not use wheels, though early adding machines did.

Try this: Watch the wheels and work out the number before you look at the ordinary digits. What is 0 0 0 0 1 0 1 1? Teacher: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · computer science, mathematics

⚙️ Inventions & Transport 24 models

A friendly three-wheeled robot with stereo sensors, ready to be programmed.

  • The word "robot" comes from a 1920 Czech play by Karel Čapek.
  • Two sensors side by side can judge distance, the same way two eyes do.
  • This robot is an invention of Edusim rather than a copy of any real product.

Real size: Imagined as a robot about as tall as a student. This model: Its own size.

Try this: Its starter program drives a square. What would you change to make a triangle?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · robotics, computer science, engineering

Leonardo da Vinci’s design for a machine that would fly by flapping its wings.

  • Leonardo drew designs like this in the late 1400s.
  • There is no record of it being built in his lifetime.
  • Human muscles are far too weak to fly a heavy machine like this, which nobody could yet have known.

Real size: Leonardo imagined a wingspan of many feet. This model: A model built from his idea.

Try this: Why do you think he studied birds before drawing this?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, engineering, art

A rounded postwar New York taxi, all curved steel and chrome.

  • Yellow cabs spread after John Hertz’s Chicago company chose the colour in 1915, reportedly because it was easy to see.
  • Cars of this era were often built on a separate steel frame.
  • This one comes from the app’s 1940s Times Square world.

Real size: About 17 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Its starter program drives it round the block. Build a road for it.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, transportation, design

A 19th-century American steam engine, with its cowcatcher, big funnel and driving rods.

  • Burning fuel boils water, and steam pushing on pistons turns the wheels.
  • Water expands to about 1,600 times its volume when it becomes steam.
  • The first railroad across the United States was completed in 1869.

Real size: About 50 feet long with its tender. This model: About half life size.

Try this: Its starter program runs it back and forth. Lay out a track for it.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

The biplane that made the first powered, controlled, sustained airplane flights in 1903.

  • Orville Wright flew it for 12 seconds and 120 feet on December 17, 1903.
  • The longest flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet.
  • Its wings spanned just over 40 feet. This model’s wires are drawn thicker than life so they can be seen.

Real size: About 40 feet across the wings. This model: About 60% of life size.

Try this: Its starter program flies a short hop. Can you beat 120 feet?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

A wooden hand press of the kind that made books affordable across Europe.

  • In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type around 1450. Korean printers had already used metal type by 1377.
  • His famous Bible was printed in the 1450s, in about 180 copies.
  • The press itself was adapted from presses already used for wine and oil.
  • No press of Gutenberg’s survives. This is the kind shown in the earliest pictures of printing.

Real size: About 6 feet tall. This model: About life size.

Try this: Why would cheaper books change who could learn to read?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, language arts, technology

The car that put America on wheels, with its upright black body, brass radiator and spoked wheels.

  • Ford built it from 1908 to 1927, and more than 15 million were made.
  • The moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, made it fast and cheap to build.
  • It stood tall on its wheels, to cope with the rough roads of the time.

Real size: About 11 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Its starter program drives it round a square. Why would an assembly line lower the price?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, transportation, engineering

A high-wheel bicycle from the 1870s, with the pedals fixed straight to its enormous front wheel.

  • With pedals on the front axle, a bigger wheel meant more distance for each turn of the pedals.
  • Its name comes from two British coins, a large penny and a small farthing.
  • Riders sat so high that a fall could be dangerous, and chain-driven bicycles replaced it.

Real size: A front wheel about 5 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Compare it with a modern bike. What job does the modern bike’s chain do?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, transportation, physics

The richly decorated blue and gold balloon that carried the first people into free flight.

  • It made the first crewed free flight, over Paris in November 1783.
  • The brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier built it.
  • Hot air is less dense than cool air, so the balloon rises.

Real size: About 75 feet tall. This model: About 1/4 of life size, with its decoration simplified.

Try this: Its starter program lifts off. Why would it come down as the air inside cools?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics

An early cylinder phonograph in a wooden case, with its crank, stylus and large horn.

  • Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877, the first machine that could play back recorded sound.
  • A needle traces a groove in the cylinder, and its vibrations reproduce the sound.
  • Sound itself is vibration, which is why this works with no electricity at all.

Real size: About 2 feet tall with its horn. This model: Enlarged about 3 times.

Try this: Why would a large horn make the sound louder?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, music

A rotative steam engine with its rocking beam, big flywheel and spinning governor.

  • James Watt’s separate condenser, patented in 1769, made steam engines far more efficient.
  • Watt also popularised the unit of horsepower, and the watt is named after him.
  • A flywheel smooths the motion, and a spinning governor controls the speed.

Real size: As big as a building. This model: A large working-style model, with its pumps left out.

Try this: Follow the motion from the piston, through the beam, to the flywheel.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

A black upright desk typewriter with its round keys, type bars, ribbon and a sheet of paper.

  • The first commercially successful typewriter went on sale in the 1870s.
  • It introduced the QWERTY layout that most computer keyboards still use.
  • Each key swings a metal letter against an inked ribbon, which prints it on the paper.

Real size: About a foot wide. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Compare its keys with a computer keyboard. Which letters are in the same place?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, language arts, technology

A three-bladed turbine on a tall white tower, with a cutaway showing the gearbox and generator.

  • Wind pushes the blades, and the turning shaft drives a generator that makes electricity. Many newer turbines drive it directly, with no gearbox.
  • Kansas is one of the leading states for wind power.
  • Large modern land turbines have towers over 300 feet tall.

Real size: Over 400 feet tall to the blade tip. This model: About 1/10 of life size, with the housing enlarged and opened so you can see inside.

Try this: Why would engineers put turbines on tall towers? Where is it windier?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · engineering, physics, earth science

A stone mill with a big wooden water wheel, one wall open to show the gears and millstones.

  • Falling water turns the wheel, and wooden gears carry that power to the millstones.
  • The stones grind grain into flour, doing work that would take many people by hand.
  • In 1086, England’s Domesday Book recorded about 6,000 water mills.

Real size: About 20 feet tall. This model: About life size.

Try this: Follow the power from the water to the millstone. How do the gears change its direction?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

An upright black and brass telephone with its rotary dial and separate earpiece on a hook.

  • Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876.
  • You spoke into the top and held the separate earpiece to your ear.
  • A microphone turns sound into a changing electric signal, and an earpiece turns it back.

Real size: About a foot tall. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Why would lifting the earpiece off its hook be how you started a call?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, technology

A one-man wooden submarine from the American Revolution, with one side cut open to show its cranks.

  • David Bushnell built the Turtle in 1775, and it is the first submarine known to have been used in combat.
  • One person worked it by hand, turning cranks for its propellers and letting water in to sink.
  • American accounts say its attack on a British warship in 1776 failed, but British records do not mention it. This model is based on later reconstructions.

Real size: About 6 to 7 feet tall, going by later reconstructions. This model: About life size.

Try this: How would letting water in, and pumping it out, make it sink and rise? Teacher: More water makes it heavier than the water it displaces, so it sinks. Pumping out makes it lighter, so it rises.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

A fast 1850s sailing ship with a sharp bow, three tall masts and a great spread of sail.

  • Clipper ships were built for speed, with long narrow hulls and huge areas of sail.
  • In 1854 the Flying Cloud sailed from New York to San Francisco in 89 days, a record for sailing ships that lasted over a century.
  • They raced to carry goods such as tea, and carried people to the California Gold Rush.

Real size: The Flying Cloud was about 225 feet long on deck. This model: About 1/10 of life size, with a rig of a slightly later style.

Try this: Why did going from New York to San Francisco by sea mean going around South America? Teacher: The Panama Canal did not open until 1914.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, geography, physics

A tall wooden longcase clock with its side open to show the gears, escapement, weights and pendulum.

  • Christiaan Huygens designed the first pendulum clock in 1656.
  • A pendulum’s swing time depends on its length, not on how heavy it is.
  • A pendulum about 39 inches long takes one second to swing each way.

Real size: About 7 feet tall. This model: Life size, with the gears lowered below the dial so you can see them. In a real clock they sit behind it.

Try this: If a clock runs slow, should you make its pendulum longer or shorter? Teacher: Shorter. A shorter pendulum swings faster.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · physics, history, engineering

A brass telegraph key and sounder wired to a battery on a wooden desk, with a printed code chart.

  • Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail sent a famous message from Washington to Baltimore in 1844.
  • Pressing the key closes a circuit, and an electromagnet at the far end clicks in response.
  • Morse code spells letters from short and long signals, called dots and dashes.

Real size: A desktop key is a few inches long. This model: Enlarged about 8 times, with both ends of the line on one desk.

Try this: Use the chart to spell your name in dots and dashes. Why would E be just one dot? Teacher: E is the most common letter in English, so giving it the shortest code saves time.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, technology, physics

The first liquid-fueled rocket in its launch frame, a spindly machine with its engine at the top.

  • Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926, in Auburn, Massachusetts.
  • It burned gasoline and liquid oxygen, and flew for about 2.5 seconds.
  • It rose only 41 feet, but it showed the way to the rockets that later reached the Moon.

Real size: About 11 feet tall. This model: About life size, with the details of its frame approximate.

Try this: Compare it with the Saturn V, which first flew only 41 years later. What changed most?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

One cylinder of a car engine cut open and running, with the piston, valves, spark plug and crankshaft moving through intake, compression, power and exhaust.

  • The four strokes are intake, compression, power and exhaust. Only the power stroke pushes the piston.
  • The crankshaft turns twice for every full set of four strokes, and a heavy flywheel carries it through the other three.
  • Nikolaus Otto built the first successful four-stroke engine in 1876.

Real size: A car engine’s cylinder is usually about 3 to 4 inches across. This model: A single cylinder about 7 feet tall, opened up to show the inside and slowed right down.

Try this: Watch the two valves. When is each one open, and when are both of them shut? Why would both need to be shut? Teacher: Both are shut for compression and power, so the mixture can be squeezed and the burning gas can only push on the piston.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · engineering, physics, technology

A hand-cranked calculating machine of brass and iron from the 1840s. Its number wheels really do work out the square numbers by adding, one turn at a time.

  • Charles Babbage designed Difference Engine No. 2 between 1847 and 1849, to work out mathematical tables without human mistakes.
  • It was not built in his lifetime. The Science Museum in London finished a working calculator from his drawings in 1991.
  • With its printer, that machine has about 8,000 parts and weighs about 5 tons. It can only add, and the method of differences turns other math into adding.

Real size: About 11 feet long and 7 feet tall. This model: About the real length, but with far fewer wheels: three columns of a few digits, where the original has eight columns of 31 digits.

Try this: Read the three columns as the crank turns. Which column stays the same, and how does it feed the others? Teacher: The right-hand column stays at 2. It adds to the middle column (3, 5, 7, 9), which adds to the left column (1, 4, 9, 16, 25), the square numbers.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · computer science, mathematics, history of science, engineering

A concrete dam in a valley, cut open down the middle, with water falling through a pipe to spin a turbine and generator, and power lines heading off to town.

  • Water held high behind a dam falls through a pipe called a penstock and spins a turbine, which turns a generator.
  • The higher the water falls and the more of it flows, the more electricity it can make.
  • A dam is thicker at the bottom because water pressure grows with depth.
  • Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, built in the 1930s, is about 726 feet tall.

Real size: From a few feet to over 700 feet tall. This model: A made-up dam on a block about 16 feet long, with the turbine and generator drawn much larger than they would be.

Try this: Follow the water from the reservoir to the river below. Where does its energy change form? Teacher: Height becomes speed in the pipe, speed becomes spinning in the turbine, and spinning becomes electricity in the generator.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · engineering, energy, physics, earth science

A beam, a truss, an arch and a suspension bridge side by side over one river, with squeezed parts painted blue and stretched parts painted red, and a truck crossing each.

  • Every bridge carries its load to the ground through parts being squeezed, called compression, and parts being stretched, called tension.
  • Stone and concrete are strong when squeezed and weak when stretched, which is why an arch can be built of stone. Steel cable is strong when stretched.
  • The longest bridge spans in the world are all suspension bridges.

Real size: From a plank over a stream to spans of more than a mile. This model: Four small models, each about 8 feet long, all crossing the same gap so that they can be compared. The red and blue paint shows the main forces and is simplified.

Try this: Pick one bridge and follow the weight of the truck to the ground. Which parts are pushed together and which are pulled apart? Teacher: On the arch, the stone is squeezed all the way to the banks. On the suspension bridge, the deck hangs from cables in tension, and the towers are squeezed.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · engineering, physics

🗺️ World Geography 16 models

A classroom globe tilted on its stand, with all seven continents and five oceans named.

  • Earth has seven continents and five oceans, and oceans cover about 71% of its surface.
  • The distance round the equator is about 24,900 miles.
  • Earth’s axis tilts about 23.4 degrees, which is why the stand holds the globe at an angle.

Real size: The real Earth is about 7,900 miles across. This model: A very small model, with no country borders so it does not go out of date.

Try this: Walk round it and find the continent you live on. Which ocean is closest to you? Teacher: Asia is the largest continent and the Pacific the largest ocean.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science

A globe wrapped in the imaginary grid that gives every place on Earth an address, with a pin to find.

  • Latitude measures how far a place is north or south of the equator, from 0 to 90 degrees.
  • Longitude measures how far east or west it is of the prime meridian, which runs through Greenwich in England.
  • One degree of latitude is about 69 miles anywhere on Earth, but degrees of longitude shrink toward the poles.

Real size: The lines are imaginary and go all the way round the Earth. This model: A very small model, with a line every 15 degrees.

Try this: Find the red pin. Read its latitude and longitude from the grid, then work out which US state it is in. Teacher: The pin is at about 38 degrees north, 97 degrees west, in Kansas.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, math

A paper map unrolling from around a globe, with Greenland and Africa marked in the same colours on both.

  • A curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching it, so every flat world map distorts something.
  • Gerardus Mercator published this projection in 1569 because it keeps compass bearings as straight lines for sailors.
  • Africa is about 14 times the area of Greenland, though on this kind of map they look much closer in size.

Real size: A wall map is usually a few feet wide. This model: A Mercator map to true proportion, stopped short of the poles, which it can never reach.

Try this: Compare Greenland and Africa on the globe, then on the map. Where on the map is the stretching worst? Teacher: Near the top and bottom: the stretching grows with distance from the equator.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, math

A globe coloured by the five main climate groups, with a key on its base.

  • Wladimir Köppen’s climate system sorts places by temperature, rainfall and the plants that grow there.
  • Its five main groups are tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.
  • Great deserts cluster near 30 degrees north and south, where dry air sinks back toward the ground.

Real size: The real Earth is about 7,900 miles across. This model: A very small model. The zones are simplified, and high mountains are not shown as their own group.

Try this: Find where you live. Then find somewhere on another continent with the same colour.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science, climate

A big brass compass with a steady needle and all sixteen named directions on its rose.

  • North, east, south and west are the four cardinal directions. Northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest fall between them.
  • A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with Earth’s magnetic field, so it points to magnetic north, which is not quite the North Pole.
  • Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so east is 90 degrees and south is 180.

Real size: A hand compass fits in a palm. This model: Greatly enlarged.

Try this: Stand at the south side of the compass and face north. Which way is west: left or right? Teacher: Left. Facing north, east is on your right and west on your left.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, navigation

Two peaks and the flat map of the same land side by side, so each line on paper can be followed on the ground.

  • A contour line joins points at the same height above sea level.
  • Lines close together mean steep ground, and lines far apart mean a gentle slope.
  • A saddle is the low point on a ridge between two peaks, and on a map it sits between two sets of closed loops.

Real size: A hill like this might be a mile or two across. This model: A small teaching model. The land and the map are drawn from the same heights.

Try this: Find the steepest side of the big peak on the map, then walk round and check it on the hill.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, math

A river fanning out to the sea, modelled on the Nile: a green triangle of farmland laid across desert.

  • A delta forms where a river slows at the sea and drops the silt it has been carrying.
  • The word comes from the Greek letter Δ, because the Nile Delta is roughly that shape.
  • Most Egyptians live along the Nile and in its delta, on a small part of the country’s land.

Real size: The Nile Delta is about 100 miles long and 150 miles wide along the coast. This model: A small teaching model with the height exaggerated and only a few of its channels.

Try this: Follow the river from the back of the block. How many times does it divide before it reaches the sea?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science

A river looping across its floodplain, wearing away one bank, building up the other, and leaving a cut-off lake behind.

  • Water runs fastest round the outside of a bend, where it wears the bank away. It slows on the inside, where it drops sand.
  • That makes each bend grow until the river cuts across the narrow neck and takes the shorter way.
  • The abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake. The word meander comes from the winding Maeander River in Turkey.

Real size: Real meanders can be many miles across. This model: A small teaching model with the height exaggerated.

Try this: Find the narrowest neck of land between two bends. What will happen to the river there? Teacher: It will break through, and the loop will be cut off as a new oxbow lake.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science

The highest mountains on Earth, wet and green to the south and a dry plateau to the north.

  • Mount Everest is the world’s highest mountain above sea level, measured in 2020 at 29,032 feet.
  • The Himalaya began rising about 40 to 50 million years ago, when India collided with Asia, and they are still rising.
  • Monsoon winds drop their rain on the southern slopes, which leaves the Tibetan Plateau to the north in a dry rain shadow.

Real size: The range is about 1,500 miles long. This model: A relief model with the height greatly exaggerated and the peaks simplified.

Try this: Compare the south side of the range with the north side. What would you pack for each?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science

A slice through the Grand Canyon, with its real rock layers named from the rim down to the river.

  • The Grand Canyon is 277 river miles long, up to 18 miles wide and about a mile deep.
  • The Colorado River cut most of the canyon in the last several million years, but the rocks it cut through are far older.
  • The dark Vishnu rocks at the bottom are about 1.7 billion years old, and the pale Kaibab Limestone on the rim is about 270 million.

Real size: About a mile deep and up to 18 miles wide. This model: A small teaching model. Each layer’s thickness and the width of the canyon are simplified.

Try this: Walk down the layers from the rim to the river. Which layers make cliffs and which make slopes? Teacher: Hard limestone and sandstone make cliffs, and soft shale wears back into slopes.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science, geology

Sand dunes around an oasis, cut open to show the buried water that keeps the palms alive.

  • The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, more than 3 million square miles.
  • Only about a quarter of it, or less, is sand. Most of the rest is bare rock and gravel.
  • An oasis forms where underground water comes close enough to the surface for plants and wells to reach it.

Real size: The largest dunes stand hundreds of feet tall. This model: A small teaching model with the height exaggerated.

Try this: Look at the front of the block. Why does the water come up here and not everywhere else? Teacher: The ground dips low enough here to reach the water-bearing rock underneath.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science

A valley carved by ice and drowned by the sea, cut open to show how deep it goes.

  • A fjord is a valley carved by a glacier and then flooded by the sea when the ice melted.
  • Norway’s Sognefjord runs about 127 miles inland and is more than 4,000 feet deep.
  • Many fjords are shallower at the mouth than further in, where a ridge of rock called a sill stands across the entrance.

Real size: The longest fjords run more than 100 miles. This model: A small teaching model with the height exaggerated.

Try this: Look at the cut face at the front. What shape is the valley under the water, and what made that shape? Teacher: A U shape, carved by a glacier. A river would have cut a V.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science

A ring of coral islands round a lagoon, cut open to show the sunken volcano underneath.

  • An atoll is a ring of coral reef and low islands round a central lagoon.
  • Charles Darwin proposed that atolls begin as reefs round a volcano, which keep growing upward as the volcano slowly sinks.
  • Drilling at Enewetak Atoll in 1952 passed through more than 4,000 feet of coral rock and reached the volcanic rock below, as he predicted.

Real size: Many atolls are a few miles to tens of miles across. This model: A small teaching model with the depth greatly compressed.

Try this: Look at the cut face at the front. Why would coral, which needs sunlight, be built on so much old coral rock? Teacher: The volcano sank slowly, and the coral kept growing upward toward the light.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, earth science, biology

A slice of the Amazon, from the river bank up through the forest’s four layers.

  • A rainforest has four layers: the emergent trees, the canopy, the understory and the forest floor.
  • The canopy is so dense that only about 2 to 5% of the sunlight reaches the forest floor.
  • The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest in the world, covering more than 2 million square miles.

Real size: Emergent trees can reach about 200 feet or more. This model: A small teaching model, with far fewer trees than a real forest so the layers can be seen.

Try this: Find a macaw. Which layer does it live in, and why might that be a good place for it?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, biology, ecology

A steep hillside turned into flooded steps, after the terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras.

  • Terraces turn a slope too steep to plough into level fields that hold water.
  • Water is led from the forest above and passes down from one field to the next.
  • The Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras, built by the Ifugao people, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.

Real size: Some of the real terraces climb thousands of feet up a mountain. This model: A small teaching model with far fewer steps than a real hillside.

Try this: Follow a drop of water from the forest to the bottom. How many fields does it pass through?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, history, agriculture

A diorama from the Queensland coast out to the Coral Sea: a turquoise map of reefs from above, and from the front an open case of corals and swimming fish, with the limestone they built in section beneath.

  • The Great Barrier Reef runs for about 1,400 miles along the coast of Queensland, Australia, and is made up of about 2,900 separate reefs and 900 islands.
  • It is the largest structure on Earth made by living things. It was built by tiny animals called coral polyps, each laying down a limestone skeleton.
  • The living reef on top is only about 6,000 to 8,000 years old. It grows on older reef rock, and complete reefs have stood here on and off for about 600,000 years.
  • Corals get much of their food and color from tiny algae living inside them. In water that stays too warm they lose the algae and turn white. This is called bleaching: a bleached coral is not dead yet, but it can starve.
  • Aboriginal Australians have lived in this region for at least 40,000 years, and Torres Strait Islanders for about 10,000. About 70 Traditional Owner groups have ties to the reef today.

Real size: About 1,400 miles long. This model: A made-up stretch on a block about 18 feet long, gathering features from different parts of the reef. Depths are squeezed, and the corals and animals are drawn far larger than the map around them.

Try this: Crouch and look at the cut face under the reef. How much of all that stone is alive? Then find the sand behind the reef and the blue beyond it. Why does the color change so fast? Teacher: Only the thin colored skin is alive. The rest is limestone left by earlier corals. The color changes because the water goes from a shallow lagoon to the very deep Coral Sea at the edge of the continental shelf.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, biology, ecology, earth science

🏙️ City Dioramas 5 models

Manhattan from the harbor to the top of Central Park: one street grid, two clusters of towers and the rivers around them.

  • The grid of avenues and numbered streets comes from the Commissioners' Plan of 1811, drawn when most of the island was still farms, hills and marshes.
  • The grid's avenues lean about 29 degrees east of true north, to fit the shape of the island.
  • Broadway is older than the grid, so it cuts across it on a diagonal and leaves wedge-shaped blocks. The Flatiron Building fills one of them.
  • Central Park is about 2.5 miles long and half a mile wide. It looks natural, but more than 20,000 workers built it, starting in the 1850s.

Real size: The area shown is about 8.5 miles from front to back and 6.5 miles across. This model: About 1 foot to half a mile, with north at the back. Landmarks sit in their true places, but streets are simplified and every building is far bigger and taller than the map scale.

Try this: Stand in the harbor and look up the island. Why do the tall towers gather in two places, with a lower city between them? Teacher: Offices cluster near their customers and each other: around the banks at the southern tip, and in midtown, where shops, theaters and hotels followed people moving north. An older explanation blames the depth of the bedrock, but researchers have found it played little part.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, history, social studies

The old city on its peninsula and the land people made around it. Warm ground was dry land in 1630, and pale ground was once water.

  • Boston was founded in 1630 on the Shawmut Peninsula, joined to the mainland by a narrow neck of land.
  • People filled in the mudflats and coves around it for centuries, with the biggest projects in the 1800s. The Back Bay was filled from 1857 and took decades.
  • Streets on the old peninsula wander, while the Back Bay's run straight, because the Back Bay was planned on paper before it was land.
  • The Freedom Trail is a red line about 2.5 miles long in the real city's pavement, linking 16 historic sites.

Real size: The area shown is about 3.7 miles across. This model: About 1 foot to a quarter of a mile, with north at the back. The 1630 shore is drawn roughly, and every building is far bigger and taller than the map scale.

Try this: Find the dashed line of the 1630 shore. Is the old John Hancock Tower standing on old land or made land? What about Fenway Park? Teacher: Both stand on made land: the tower on the filled Back Bay and the ballpark on filled marshland in the Fenway.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, history, social studies

The Thames, the Roman town at its crossing and the palaces upriver: a city with two centers and no single plan.

  • The Romans founded Londinium soon after invading Britain in AD 43, at a place where they could bridge the Thames.
  • London grew from two centers: the City, the trading town inside the old Roman wall, and Westminster upriver, the seat of kings and Parliament.
  • After the Great Fire of 1666, Christopher Wren proposed a new street plan, but the city was rebuilt largely along its old streets. His St Paul's Cathedral rose in the middle of it.
  • Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell. The tower that holds it is the Elizabeth Tower.

Real size: The area shown is about 5 miles across. This model: About 1 foot to a third of a mile, with north at the back. The Roman wall is drawn roughly, and every building is far bigger and taller than the map scale.

Try this: Find the dashed line of the Roman wall, then find the cluster of modern towers north of the river. What do you notice? Teacher: The towers stand in and beside the City of London, the old Roman town, which is still a center of banking and trade nearly two thousand years on.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, history, social studies

The Seine, its islands and the wide straight boulevards that were cut through the old city in the 1850s and 1860s.

  • From 1853 to 1870, Georges-Eugene Haussmann, working for Napoleon III, cut wide straight boulevards through the crowded medieval streets.
  • Building rules older than Haussmann, updated in his time, tied a building's height to the width of its street. That, with pale limestone and grey roofs, is why so much of Paris matches.
  • Twelve avenues meet at the Arc de Triomphe, in a circle long known as the Etoile, French for star.
  • Soon after the Montparnasse Tower was finished in 1973, the city banned buildings of that height from central Paris.

Real size: The area shown is about 4 miles across. This model: About 1 foot to a quarter of a mile, with north at the back. Only the main boulevards are drawn, some landmarks are nudged to fit, and every building is far bigger and taller than the map scale.

Try this: Stand at the Arc de Triomphe and follow the Champs-Elysees. What lies along that straight line? Teacher: The Champs-Elysees runs to the Place de la Concorde, and the same line carries on through the Tuileries Gardens to the Louvre. It is called the historical axis.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, history, social studies

A city that grew outward in rings from one fortress beside the Moskva River.

  • A kremlin is a fortress inside a Russian city. Moscow's brick walls were built mainly from 1485 to 1495, with Italian architects in charge.
  • St Basil's Cathedral was built from 1555 to 1561 on the orders of Ivan the Terrible, to mark the capture of Kazan.
  • The Boulevard Ring and the Garden Ring follow old walls and earth ramparts, pulled down once the city had outgrown them. Main roads cross them like the spokes of a wheel.
  • The tall stepped towers are three of the seven Stalin-era high-rises begun around 1947, nicknamed in English the Seven Sisters.

Real size: The area shown is about 3.4 miles across. This model: About 1 foot to a fifth of a mile, with north at the back. The Kremlin and Red Square are enlarged, the roads are simplified, and every building is far bigger and taller than the map scale.

Try this: Walk the green Boulevard Ring from one end to the other. Where does it stop? Then follow a straight road outward from the Kremlin. What does it cross? Teacher: The Boulevard Ring is really a horseshoe whose two ends stop near the river, leaving the south side open. The roads running outward cross each ring in turn, like a spider's web.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, history, social studies

🏛️ Landmarks 24 models

A lion with a human head, carved from the limestone of the Giza plateau.

  • It is about 240 feet long and 66 feet high.
  • It was carved around 4,500 years ago, and most scholars link it to the pharaoh Khafre.
  • Its nose has been missing for centuries.

Real size: About 240 feet long. This model: About 1/12 of life size.

Try this: Place a Pyramid of Giza behind it and arrange them like the real plateau.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, art

The largest pyramid at Giza, its courses of stone exposed where the casing has gone.

  • It was built around 2560 BCE for the pharaoh Khufu.
  • It was the tallest structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years.
  • It contains an estimated 2.3 million stone blocks.

Real size: Originally about 481 feet tall. This model: About 1/24 of life size.

Try this: A square base and four triangles: try building one yourself with Create Model.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, mathematics, world cultures

Rome’s great amphitheatre, tiers of arches round an oval arena.

  • It opened in the year 80 CE.
  • It held around 50,000 spectators.
  • Its oval measures about 615 by 510 feet, and its walls rise about 157 feet.

Real size: About 615 feet long. This model: About 1/25 of life size.

Try this: Compare its arches with a modern stadium. What has changed, and what has not?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, engineering

A gift from the people of France, standing on its pedestal in New York Harbor.

  • It was dedicated in 1886.
  • The statue is about 151 feet tall, and about 305 feet from the ground to the torch.
  • It is copper, and it turned green as the surface weathered.

Real size: About 305 feet tall with its pedestal. This model: About 1/18 of life size.

Try this: What might it have meant to people arriving by ship at Ellis Island?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, civics, art

The white marble mausoleum built at Agra in memory of Mumtaz Mahal.

  • The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it in memory of his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
  • The whole complex was finished around 1653.
  • It stands about 240 feet tall, and its marble seems to change colour with the light.

Real size: About 240 feet tall. This model: About 1/13 of life size.

Try this: Look at it from all four sides. What do you notice about its symmetry?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, art

The marble temple to Athena on the Acropolis of Athens, roofless and weathered.

  • It was built between 447 and 432 BCE.
  • Its outer colonnade has 46 Doric columns: 8 across each end and 17 along each side.
  • The columns swell slightly, a subtle curve called entasis. It is exaggerated here so you can see it.
  • All 46 columns stand in this model so they can be counted. On the real temple, parts of the colonnade are broken.

Real size: About 228 feet long. This model: About 1/8 of life size.

Try this: Count the columns along one side, remembering not to count the corners twice.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, art, mathematics

A stone castle with a central keep, a curtain wall, four towers and a gatehouse.

  • This is a typical design rather than one particular castle.
  • A strong central tower called the keep was the last place to hold in an attack.
  • Round towers have no corners for attackers to undermine, so they are harder to bring down.

Real size: A castle like this could be 200 feet across. This model: About 1/8 of life size.

Try this: Where would you attack this castle? Where would you defend it?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, engineering

The wrought-iron tower in Paris, with its four arched legs and open lattice all the way up.

  • It was built for the 1889 World’s Fair in Paris.
  • It is about 1,083 feet tall, and it was the tallest structure in the world until 1930.
  • Its open lattice lets the wind pass through instead of pushing against it.

Real size: About 1,083 feet tall. This model: About 1/30 of life size.

Try this: Why would an open lattice be better than a solid wall in strong wind?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, engineering

A stretch of the Ming wall climbing a rocky ridge, with its battlements and two watchtowers.

  • Sections were built over about 2,000 years by several dynasties.
  • Most of the famous stone and brick stretches were built in the Ming dynasty.
  • Despite the popular claim, it is not easy to see from space with the naked eye.

Real size: All its sections total more than 13,000 miles. This model: One short stretch, about 1/8 of life size.

Try this: How would watchtowers within sight of each other send a warning quickly?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, geography

The white marble bell tower in Italy, with eight storeys of arches and its famous lean.

  • Building began in 1173, and it started to lean during construction because the ground was soft.
  • Engineers reduced the lean to about 4 degrees by removing soil under the high side.
  • It is about 185 feet tall.

Real size: About 185 feet tall. This model: About 1/8 of life size.

Try this: Use Rotate/Move Shape to stand the tower straight. What happens to the ground around it?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, physics

The prehistoric stone circle in England as it stands today, with its great trilithons.

  • Its large stones were put up around 2500 BCE.
  • The smaller bluestones came from Wales, about 150 miles away.
  • It lines up with sunrise at the summer solstice. Nobody knows all of what it was for.

Real size: The stone circle is about 100 feet across. This model: Stones about 1/4 of life size, with the bank, ditch and Heel Stone moved closer.

Try this: With no machines, how might people have moved a 25-ton stone?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, astronomy

The stepped Maya pyramid in Mexico, with a staircase on all four sides and a temple on top.

  • The Maya built it at Chichén Itzá, on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, about a thousand years ago.
  • Each of its four stairways has 91 steps, and with the top platform that makes 365.
  • At the equinoxes, shadows on its stairway look like a serpent moving down the pyramid.

Real size: About 98 feet tall. This model: About 1/6 of life size.

Try this: Why might people who tracked the sky build 365 into a building?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, mathematics, astronomy

The red-orange suspension bridge, with its two towers and sweeping cables, over a slice of bay.

  • It opened in 1937, and its main span was the longest in the world until 1964.
  • Its main span is 4,200 feet, and its towers rise 746 feet above the water.
  • The two main cables hold up the deck, passing the load to the towers and anchorages.

Real size: About 1.7 miles long. This model: About 1/200 of life size, with the towers, deck and cables thickened.

Try this: Find where the cables are lowest and highest. Why would they hang in that curve?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, engineering, physics

A temple-like front carved straight out of a rose-red cliff in Jordan.

  • The Nabataean people carved it from the sandstone cliff about 2,000 years ago.
  • It was not built up from blocks: its carvers cut it down out of the solid rock.
  • Despite the name, it was probably a royal tomb and not a treasury.

Real size: About 130 feet tall. This model: About 1/6 of life size.

Try this: Why would carving from the top down be easier than starting at the bottom?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, art

The white sail-like shells of the concert hall on its point in Sydney Harbour.

  • Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the design competition in 1957, and it opened in 1973.
  • Its shells are covered in more than a million cream and white tiles.
  • Working out how to build the curved shells was one of the hardest parts of the project.

Real size: About 600 feet long. This model: About 1/20 of life size.

Try this: What shapes can you see in the shells? They all come from parts of one sphere.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · art, engineering, world cultures

The great temple of Cambodia, with its five lotus-bud towers, galleries and surrounding moat.

  • The Khmer king Suryavarman II built it in the early 1100s, first as a Hindu temple.
  • It later became a Buddhist site, and it is on Cambodia’s national flag.
  • Its moat, wider than a football field is long, surrounds the whole temple.

Real size: The central tower is over 200 feet tall. This model: About 1/20 of life size, with the moat and grounds drawn in closer.

Try this: Count the towers from the front and then from a corner. Why might they look different? Teacher: There are five towers. From directly in front, only three can be seen clearly.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, art

The Great Enclosure of the medieval African city, with its curved granite walls and conical tower.

  • Ancestors of the Shona people built this stone city from about the 11th to the 15th centuries.
  • Its granite walls stand up to about 36 feet tall, and were built with no mortar at all.
  • It grew rich on trade in gold and ivory, and the country of Zimbabwe takes its name from it.

Real size: The wall of the Great Enclosure is about 820 feet around. This model: About 1/12 of life size, with its doorways and passage widened.

Try this: How could a wall this tall stay up with nothing holding the stones together? Teacher: Carefully fitted stones and the weight of the wall hold it together, and its thick base leans slightly inward.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, engineering

The Art Deco skyscraper of New York, stepping back as it rises to its slender mast.

  • It was finished in 1931, after just over a year of construction.
  • Its roof is 1,250 feet up, and it was the world’s tallest building for almost 40 years.
  • Its setbacks, which step the building in as it rises, let light reach the streets below.

Real size: About 1,454 feet tall to the tip of its antenna. This model: About 1/35 of life size.

Try this: Why would a city want tall buildings to get narrower as they rise?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, engineering, art

The white hilltop castle of Japan, with its great main keep and layered curving roofs.

  • Its great main keep was finished in about 1609.
  • It is nicknamed the White Heron Castle, after its white plaster walls and its graceful shape.
  • It was never attacked in battle, and it survived bombing in World War II and a big earthquake in 1995. It became a World Heritage Site in 1993.

Real size: The main keep is about 150 feet tall. This model: About 1/10 of life size, with its grounds drawn in closer.

Try this: Place a Medieval Castle beside it. How are their ideas of defence alike and different?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, engineering

The vast mud-brick building of Mali, its towers bristling with palm-wood beams.

  • It is the largest mud-brick building in the world, and the present building dates from 1907.
  • The bundles of palm wood sticking out of its walls strengthen them, and serve as scaffolding.
  • Each year the people of Djenné gather to replaster it with fresh mud, in a great community festival.

Real size: Its platform is about 250 feet on each side. This model: About 1/10 of life size.

Try this: Why would a building of mud need looking after every year, and why might a whole town help?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, art, engineering

The domed home of Congress in Washington, D.C., with its long wings for the Senate and the House.

  • Congress meets here: the Senate in the north wing and the House of Representatives in the south wing.
  • George Washington laid its cornerstone in 1793.
  • Its cast-iron dome was built during the 1850s and 1860s, and work went on through the Civil War.

Real size: About 288 feet tall to the top of the statue. This model: About 1/20 of life size.

Try this: Why would a country want its lawmakers to meet in one building with two separate wings? Teacher: Congress has two chambers, the Senate and the House, and each has its own wing.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · civics, history, art

The great three-tier Roman bridge over the Gard, with its top channel opened up so you can see the water flowing along to the city.

  • It carried water across a river valley to the Roman city of Nemausus, now Nîmes in France, and was built in the first century CE.
  • It is about 160 feet tall. Its top tier of 35 small arches is about 900 feet long.
  • There were no pumps. The channel sloped down the whole way, on average by only about 1 foot in every 3,000.
  • It was built largely without mortar, and some of its blocks weigh up to 6 tons.

Real size: About 160 feet tall and 900 feet long across the top. This model: About 1/20 size, and shortened to show fewer arches, with a length of the top channel opened up.

Try this: Why would builders stack three rows of arches instead of building one solid wall? Think about stone, cost, and the river. Teacher: Arches use much less stone while carrying the load down the piers, and they let the river flow through, even in a flood.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, engineering, ancient rome

The great stepped tower of Sumer, in mud brick with its three staircases meeting at a gateway, drawn with the upper levels archaeologists believe it had.

  • King Ur-Nammu began it around 2100 BCE, in what is now southern Iraq, for Nanna, the moon god of the city of Ur.
  • Its core is mud brick, faced with baked brick set in bitumen, a natural tar.
  • Its base is about 210 feet by 150 feet.
  • Only the lowest level survives well. The upper levels shown here are a reconstruction, based on Leonard Woolley’s digs of the 1920s and 1930s.

Real size: About 210 by 150 feet at the base, and perhaps 70 to 100 feet tall when new. This model: About 1/20 size. The upper levels and the shrine are an informed reconstruction, not known for certain.

Try this: Look at the holes in the walls of the lowest level. The core behind them is mud brick, which holds water. What might they be for? Teacher: They are thought to have let moisture escape from the mud-brick core as it dried out between rains.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, ancient mesopotamia, architecture

The whole Giza Plateau around 2500 BCE, with the pyramids still in their white casing, the Sphinx, temples, tombs, the builders’ town and boats in the harbor, beside the Great Pyramid cut in half to show its chambers.

  • The three great pyramids were built for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, between about 2600 and 2500 BCE.
  • A pyramid was only the end of a complex. A valley temple stood at the water, and a long covered causeway climbed to a mortuary temple beside the pyramid.
  • The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years. It has about 2.3 million blocks, and its sides line up with north, south, east and west to about a tenth of a degree.
  • Modern evidence points to conscripted laborers rather than slaves. Archaeologists have found their town south of the Sphinx, with sleeping quarters, bakeries, kitchens and workshops.
  • Papyri found at Wadi al-Jarf in 2013 include a diary by an inspector named Merer, who recorded carrying limestone from Tura to Giza by boat.
  • The white casing is nearly all gone now, carted away after medieval earthquakes, which is why the pyramids look stepped and brown today.

Real size: The Great Pyramid was about 481 feet tall, and the monuments here spread across about a mile. This model: The positions follow the real plan, with north at the back. The monuments are drawn 1.4 times larger than the plan, and heights of the ground are squeezed. The harbor, the Nile channel and some of the town are informed reconstructions: the river really lay farther east. The cutaway is to its own, larger scale, and its passages are drawn on one plane, though the entrance is really about 25 feet east of the center line.

Try this: Stand at the front and pick the taller of the two big pyramids. Then read their signs and the card. Why might your eyes be fooled? After that, follow one block of stone from the harbor to the top of the Great Pyramid. Teacher: Khafre’s pyramid looks taller because it stands on higher ground, but Khufu’s, the Great Pyramid, was taller: about 481 feet against about 471.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, mathematics, engineering

🏺 History & Artifacts 19 models

An instrument of rings that models the great circles of the sky around the Earth.

  • Instruments of rings like this were used in ancient Greece and in ancient China.
  • Each ring stands for a circle in the sky, such as the celestial equator or the Sun’s yearly path.
  • This one puts Earth at the centre, as most astronomers did before Copernicus.

Real size: Usually from about a foot to several feet tall. This model: A large display model.

Try this: Find the tilted ring. It marks the path the Sun appears to follow through the year.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history of science, astronomy

A broken stone slab carrying one decree in three scripts, the key to reading hieroglyphs.

  • It carries a decree of 196 BCE in hieroglyphs, Demotic and ancient Greek.
  • It was found in 1799, and Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.
  • The writing on this model is representative: it shows the three scripts’ look rather than the real text.

Real size: About 44 inches tall and weighing about 1,700 pounds. This model: About twice life size.

Try this: Why does having the same message in a known language help you read an unknown one?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, language arts, world cultures

A clinker-built Norse ship with a square sail, shields and a row of oar ports.

  • Overlapping planks made the hull light and flexible.
  • A shallow hull let longships sail far up rivers as well as across seas.
  • Norse sailors reached North America around the year 1000.

Real size: The Gokstad ship is about 76 feet long. This model: About 1/3 of life size.

Try this: Its starter program sails it back and forth. Build it a shore to land on.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, engineering

A two-handled storage jar decorated in the black-figure style.

  • Amphorae stored and carried wine, olive oil and other goods.
  • The word means "carried on both sides", after its two handles.
  • In black-figure painting, figures were painted in slip that turned black in the kiln.

Real size: About 1 to 2 feet tall. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Stretch it wider and taller. What would each shape be better at holding?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, art, world cultures

A suanpan, the Chinese counting frame, with beads on rods in two decks.

  • Each rod is one place value, like the columns of a written number.
  • A bead above the beam counts five, and a bead below counts one.
  • Skilled users can still calculate astonishingly quickly on one.

Real size: About a foot wide. This model: Enlarged about 6 times.

Try this: Beads moved to the beam are the ones that count. Which number is it showing? Teacher: It shows 7,295. The rightmost rod is the ones.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · mathematics, history, world cultures

A prairie schooner, the canvas-topped wagon of the overland trails.

  • The Oregon Trail ran about 2,000 miles, and the journey took around five months.
  • Most travellers walked beside the wagon to spare the animals.
  • Oxen were the commonest team, since they were strong and could live on prairie grass.

Real size: A box about 10 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: A wagon could carry about a ton. What would you pack, and what would you leave?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, geography

A wooden siege engine with a heavy counterweight, a long throwing arm and a sling.

  • A falling counterweight swings the long arm, and a sling adds to the speed of the stone.
  • It turns the stored energy of a raised weight into the motion of a thrown stone.
  • Large ones could throw stones of well over 100 pounds at castle walls.

Real size: The largest may have stood over 50 feet tall. This model: About 1/3 of life size.

Try this: Place it across from a Medieval Castle. What would make it throw further?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

The cracked bronze bell of Philadelphia, hanging in its wooden yoke on a stand.

  • It was cast in the 1750s for what is now Independence Hall in Philadelphia.
  • Its inscription reads "Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land".
  • People campaigning to end slavery gave it the name Liberty Bell in the 1830s.

Real size: About 3 feet tall and over 2,000 pounds. This model: About twice life size.

Try this: Why do you think people who wanted to end slavery chose this bell as a symbol?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, civics

A full suit of 15th-century steel plate armor on a display stand, with its visor raised.

  • A full suit weighed about 50 pounds, about the same as the kit modern firefighters carry.
  • Its weight was spread over the whole body, so a trained knight could run and climb.
  • Overlapping plates let the joints bend, like the sections of a lobster’s tail.

Real size: About the height of a person. This model: Life size.

Try this: Look at the elbow and knee. How do the plates let them bend?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, engineering

A Japanese suit of lacquered plates laced with silk, seated on a storage chest as it is displayed.

  • Samurai armor was made of many small lacquered plates, laced together with silk cord.
  • Lacing made it flexible. Some suits were lighter than European plate armor, but the largest weighed as much or more.
  • Helmets, called kabuto, often carried a crest that made the wearer easy to recognise.

Real size: About the height of a person. This model: Life size.

Try this: Place a Suit of Knight’s Armor beside it. What is different, and why might that be?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures

A clay tablet pressed with rows of wedge-shaped marks, the earliest known writing system.

  • Cuneiform began in Mesopotamia, now mostly in Iraq, more than 5,000 years ago.
  • Scribes pressed a cut reed into wet clay, and the name means "wedge-shaped".
  • Many of the earliest tablets are records of goods, such as grain and sheep. The marks on this model are representative.

Real size: Many would fit in your palm. This model: Enlarged about 12 times.

Try this: Why would keeping track of grain and sheep be a reason to invent writing?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, language arts, world cultures

A main cord hung with coloured strings tied in knots, the Inca way of keeping records.

  • The Inca recorded information with knotted cords called quipu, or khipu.
  • Many use base ten: the position of a knot along the cord gives its place value.
  • Scholars can read the numbers on many of them, and are still working out what the rest record.
  • Some cords hold the sum of a group of others, as the last cord of each group does here.

Real size: Cords a foot or two long. This model: Enlarged about 3 times, with every knot tied separately so it can be counted.

Try this: Knots near the top count hundreds, then tens, then ones. Read one cord. Teacher: The first cord from the left reads 352: three knots, then five, then two. The groups total 744, 406 and 367.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, mathematics, world cultures

A light two-wheeled racing chariot of wood and leather, with its yoke and team colours.

  • Chariot racing was hugely popular in ancient Rome, and teams were known by their colours.
  • The Circus Maximus in Rome could hold well over 100,000 spectators.
  • Racing chariots were kept very light, so that the horses could run faster. This model has no horses.

Real size: No real one survives, so its size is estimated from small bronze models and carvings. This model: About life size, with its painting and details a best guess.

Try this: Why would two wheels and light wood matter for a race? What about on a sharp turn?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, physics

A blue and white Chinese porcelain jar, painted with a dragon among clouds and waves.

  • The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, and its blue and white porcelain became famous worldwide.
  • The blue comes from cobalt, painted on before the glaze and the firing.
  • Porcelain is fired so hot that it becomes hard, white and slightly see-through when thin.

Real size: About 1 to 2 feet tall. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Why do you think English speakers came to call fine porcelain "china"?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · art, history, world cultures

A pierced brass star-map instrument hanging on a stand, used for finding the time from the stars.

  • Astrolabes began with the ancient Greeks and were greatly developed in the medieval Islamic world.
  • The pierced top plate is a map of bright stars, which turns over a plate engraved for one latitude.
  • Sighting a star along the back told its height, and from that its user could work out the time.

Real size: Usually a hand-sized disc. This model: Enlarged about 8 times, with its star map computed for Kansas and its ornament representative.

Try this: Why would one plate only work at one latitude? Think about which stars you can see from Kansas.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history of science, astronomy, mathematics

A Great Plains settler’s home built from blocks of prairie turf, with a small garden and a stovepipe.

  • The Homestead Act of 1862 drew settlers to the Great Plains, where there were very few trees to build with.
  • They cut the tough prairie turf into blocks, and stacked them like bricks.
  • Thick walls kept these houses cool in summer and warm in winter, though their roofs often leaked.

Real size: About 16 feet wide. This model: About life size.

Try this: What would be good about living in this house? What would be hard?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, geography, science

A bronze urn with eight dragons holding balls above eight open-mouthed toads, to signal an earthquake.

  • The Chinese scholar Zhang Heng built the first known earthquake detector in the year 132.
  • A shake made a dragon drop its ball into the toad below, and that was said to show the direction of the quake.
  • None survives and its inner workings are unknown, so models like this one are based on old descriptions.

Real size: Described as about 6 feet across. This model: About life size.

Try this: Count the dragons. How would eight dragons help tell where a far-off earthquake came from? Teacher: There are eight, facing the eight main compass directions.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history of science, earth science, world cultures

A long pole on a pivot with a bucket at one end and a mud counterweight at the other, beside a canal.

  • A shaduf lifts water from a river or canal to water crops, using a lever and a counterweight.
  • Tomb paintings show them in ancient Egypt, and they were used in Mesopotamia even earlier.
  • Farmers still use them in some places today.

Real size: A pole often 10 to 15 feet long. This model: About life size.

Try this: Why would the heavy weight make lifting a full bucket easier? What job does the person do? Teacher: The weight does the lifting. The person pulls the empty bucket down into the water.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, world cultures

An ancient Greek warship with three banks of oars, a bronze ram, a painted eye and a square sail.

  • A trireme had three levels of oars, worked by about 170 rowers.
  • Its main weapon was the bronze ram on its bow.
  • Athenian triremes helped defeat the Persian fleet at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE.

Real size: About 120 feet long. This model: About 1/3 of life size, with each tier’s oar blades painted differently so they can be counted.

Try this: Why would three levels of oars be better than one long row? Think about the length of the ship. Teacher: It packs in more rowers, and so more speed and power, without making the ship much longer.

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, world cultures, engineering

🎻 Arts & Music 19 models

A concert grand with its lid raised, showing the strings and soundboard inside.

  • Bartolomeo Cristofori built the first pianos in Italy around 1700.
  • A modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
  • Each key throws a felt hammer at its strings, so a piano is both a string and a percussion instrument.

Real size: A concert grand is about 9 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Look at how the strings get shorter toward the high notes.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, physics, history

A violin and bow on a stand, with its scroll, f-holes and four strings.

  • Its four strings are tuned to G, D, A and E.
  • The violin took its modern form in Italy in the 1500s.
  • Antonio Stradivari’s violins from around 1700 are among the most valued instruments in the world.

Real size: About 23 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Why do you think its body is hollow? What would a solid one sound like?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, physics, history

A goblet-shaped drum from West Africa, carved from one log and tuned with rope.

  • The djembe comes from West Africa and is closely linked with the Mandinka people.
  • It gives three main sounds: a deep bass, a tone and a sharp slap.
  • Its name is often explained by a saying: "anke djé, anke bé", meaning "everyone gather together".

Real size: About 2 feet tall. This model: Enlarged about 2 times.

Try this: Its shape works like a bottle. Where does the deep sound come from?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, world cultures

A wooden studio easel holding a canvas, with a palette of mixed paint beside it.

  • The canvas shows a colour wheel: primary colours, and the secondary colours they mix to make.
  • Colours opposite each other on the wheel are called complementary.
  • Easels may go back as far as ancient Egypt, and a Roman writer mentioned one about 2,000 years ago.

Real size: About 6 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Which two primaries mix to make the colour opposite red?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · art, history

A six-string guitar on a stand, with its sound hole, bridge and fretted neck.

  • Its six strings are usually tuned E, A, D, G, B and E.
  • Pressing a string behind a fret shortens the part that vibrates, which raises the note.
  • The hollow body makes the sound of the strings louder.

Real size: About 3 feet long. This model: About twice life size.

Try this: Find the thickest string. Is it the highest note or the lowest? Teacher: The thickest string plays the lowest note.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, physics

A gilded pedal harp with 47 strings, its curved neck, carved column and seven pedals.

  • A modern concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals.
  • The red strings are all Cs and the dark ones are all Fs, so that the player can find their place.
  • Harps are among the oldest instruments, shown in art from ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.

Real size: About 6 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Compare the longest and shortest strings. Which plays the higher note? Teacher: The shortest string plays the highest note.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, history, physics

A brass trumpet on a stand, with its three valves, looped tubing and flared bell.

  • The player makes the sound by buzzing their lips into the mouthpiece.
  • Pressing a valve sends the air through extra tubing, which lowers the note.
  • Its tubing would be about 4.5 feet long if it were straightened out.

Real size: About 19 inches long. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Trace the tubing from the mouthpiece to the bell. Why is it looped?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, physics

An Indian long-necked lute on a stand, with its gourd body, arched frets and inlaid decoration.

  • The sitar is a leading instrument of North Indian classical music.
  • It usually has about 18 to 21 strings, though only some are plucked.
  • The rest ring by themselves when nearby notes are played. These are called sympathetic strings.

Real size: About 4 feet long. This model: About twice life size.

Try this: Find the strings running under the frets. Why would they ring without being touched?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, world cultures, physics

The masks of comedy and tragedy on a stand, the classic symbols of the theatre.

  • Actors in ancient Athens wore masks, and these two faces became the symbols of theatre.
  • A small group of actors could play many parts by changing masks.
  • Greek plays were performed outdoors in the 5th century BCE, for audiences of thousands.

Real size: About the size of a face. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Why would a big, clear expression matter for someone in the back row?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · drama, history, language arts

The open-air London playhouse where Shakespeare’s plays were staged, with its thatched galleries and stage.

  • The Globe was built in London in 1599, and it could hold about 3,000 people.
  • It burned down in 1613, when a stage cannon set fire to the thatch.
  • Cheap tickets bought a place standing in the open yard, right beside the stage.

Real size: About 100 feet across. This model: About 1/5 of life size.

Try this: Where would you stand if you had only a penny? Where if you were rich?

Grades 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · language arts, drama, history

An open handwritten book on a slanted desk, with a gold initial, a quill pen and an inkwell.

  • Before printing, every book was copied by hand, and one could take many months.
  • Pages were usually parchment, made from animal skin.
  • "Illuminated" refers to the bright decoration, often with real gold. The text on this model is representative.

Real size: A page about a foot tall. This model: Enlarged about 4 times.

Try this: Place a Gutenberg Printing Press beside it. What changed for people who wanted a book?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · language arts, art, history

A wooden kick wheel with a half-formed pot on it, beside a stool and finished pots.

  • Potter’s wheels were in use in the ancient Near East more than 5,000 years ago.
  • The spinning wheel lets a potter shape even, round pots quickly.
  • A heavy flywheel at the bottom keeps it turning between kicks.

Real size: About 3.5 feet tall with the pot. This model: Life size.

Try this: Why would a heavy wheel keep spinning longer than a light one?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · art, history, physics

A five-piece drum kit with a bass drum, snare, toms, hi-hat and cymbals, set up to play.

  • A kit lets one person play many drums, using both hands and both feet.
  • The kit grew up in American theatre, ragtime and jazz bands, helped by a reliable bass drum pedal patented in 1909.
  • Wires under the snare drum rattle against it, which gives its sharp sound.
