Real size: About 6 feet wide. This model: Life size.

Try this: Find the biggest and smallest drums. Which plays the deepest note? Teacher: The biggest, the bass drum, plays the deepest note.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, physics

A concert marimba with rosewood bars laid out like a piano keyboard, tube resonators and a set of mallets.

  • Its ancestors most likely came from Africa, and it became central to the music of Central America.
  • Longer bars play lower notes, and a tube under each bar makes its sound louder.
  • Its bars are laid out like the keys of a piano.

Real size: About 7 to 8 feet wide. This model: Life size.

Try this: Compare the bars with the tubes under them. What do you notice about their lengths? Teacher: Both get longer toward the low notes.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, world cultures, physics

A long Japanese zither of paulownia wood, with 13 strings and tall movable bridges.

  • The koto came to Japan from China more than 1,000 years ago.
  • Its 13 strings are each raised on a movable bridge, which is shifted to tune it.
  • Players pluck it with picks worn on the thumb and two fingers.

Real size: About 6 feet long. This model: About life size, with its strings and picks a little enlarged.

Try this: How would moving a bridge change a string’s note? Teacher: Moving it changes the length of string that vibrates. A shorter length plays a higher note.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, world cultures

A polished brass alto saxophone on a stand, with its curved neck, cone-shaped body and many keys.

  • The Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax patented it in 1846.
  • It is made of brass but counts as a woodwind, because a reed makes the sound.
  • Its tube widens steadily along its length, in the shape of a long cone.

Real size: An alto is about 2 feet tall. This model: Enlarged about 3 times.

Try this: Compare it with the Trumpet. Why would one count as brass and the other as a woodwind? Teacher: A trumpet player buzzes their lips, and a saxophone player vibrates a reed.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, history, physics

A West African harp-lute with a large calabash body, a long neck and 21 strings in two rows.

  • The kora is played in West Africa, especially by griots, who keep history and stories alive in song.
  • It has 21 strings, once made from thin strips of hide and now usually fishing line or harp string, and a body cut from a large gourd.
  • The player holds it facing them and plucks with the thumbs and forefingers of both hands.

Real size: About 4 feet tall. This model: About one and a half times life size.

Try this: How is this different from the Concert Harp? Why would a history-keeper want something portable?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, world cultures, history

A chromed tenor pan on its stand, with its bowl hammered into a pattern of note shapes.

  • The steelpan was invented in Trinidad and Tobago in the 1930s and 1940s, and is its national instrument.
  • The first pans were made from metal containers like biscuit tins and paint cans. Empty oil drums took over in the 1940s.
  • Each note is a separate hammered patch of the bowl, and smaller patches play higher notes.

Real size: About 2 feet across. This model: Enlarged about 2 times.

Try this: Find the biggest and smallest note shapes. Which plays the highest note? Teacher: The smallest shape plays the highest note.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, world cultures, physics

A large gold-lacquered tuba on a stand, with its coiled tubing, four valves and upward-facing bell.

  • The tuba is the largest and lowest-pitched brass instrument.
  • It was patented in Berlin in 1835.
  • A large B-flat tuba has about 18 feet of tubing if straightened, which is why it plays such low notes.

Real size: About 3 feet tall. This model: About twice life size.

Try this: Place a Trumpet beside it. How does the length of tubing change the note? Teacher: Longer tubing plays lower notes.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · music, physics, history

🏡 Build a Village 25 models

A snug whitewashed cottage with a deep thatched roof, a door you can walk through and one room inside.

  • Thatch is made from tightly packed reed, straw or grass.
  • Its steep slope sends rain running off before it can soak in.
  • A thick layer of thatch traps air, which helps keep a house warm in winter and cool in summer.

Real size: About 24 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Start your village here. Which way should the door face, toward the well or toward the fields? Why?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, geography, engineering

A one-room cabin of notched logs with a stone chimney, a porch and a door you can walk through.

  • Swedish and Finnish settlers brought log building to North America in the 1600s.
  • Notches cut near the ends of the logs lock the corners together, with no nails needed.
  • Gaps between the logs were stuffed with clay, moss or wood chips, called chinking.

Real size: About 20 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Log cabins were built where trees were plentiful. What should you plant or place nearby so your village has wood?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, geography, engineering

A flat-roofed house of sun-dried mud brick, with roof beams showing, a ladder to the roof and a round outdoor oven.

  • Adobe bricks are made of earth, water and straw, and are dried in the sun rather than baked in a kiln.
  • Thick earth walls heat up slowly, so the rooms stay cooler by day and warmer at night.
  • The adobe homes of Taos Pueblo in New Mexico have been lived in for hundreds of years, and the Taos people have called this valley home for about a thousand.

Real size: About 20 feet across. This model: Life size.

Try this: Adobe suits a hot, dry place. What would happen to these walls in a very rainy village? Teacher: Unprotected mud brick softens and washes away in heavy rain, so adobe needs regular replastering and works best in dry climates.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, geography, science, world cultures

A wood and bamboo house raised high on posts, with a ladder, a broad thatched roof and shade underneath.

  • Stilt houses are built in many flood-prone and tropical places, including Southeast Asia and the Amazon.
  • Raising the floor keeps the home above floodwater and lets cool air flow underneath.
  • The shady space below is often used for working, storing tools or keeping animals.

Real size: About 20 feet long and 20 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Put this beside your stream. Which of your other houses would you least like to be in during a flood? Teacher: The houses built on the ground, especially the adobe one, whose walls can be damaged by standing water.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · geography, science, world cultures, engineering

A big gambrel-roofed barn with sliding doors, stalls you can walk into and hay stacked in the loft.

  • A gambrel roof has two slopes on each side, which leaves much more room for hay in the loft.
  • Hay stored in the loft stays dry and is easy to drop down to the animals below.
  • Many old barns were painted with homemade paint coloured with red iron oxide, because it was cheap.

Real size: About 40 feet long and 30 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Which of your animals go in the barn, and how far is it from there to the crops they eat? Move things until the walk is short.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, science, engineering

A white clapboard school with a bell on the roof, and rows of desks, a stove and a blackboard inside.

  • One teacher taught every grade together in one room, and older students often helped younger ones.
  • In 1919 the United States still had about 190,000 one-room schools.
  • A bell on the roof called children in to start the school day.

Real size: About 30 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: Walk inside and count the desks. If your village has this many children, how many homes should it have? Teacher: There is no single answer. Students should explain the number of children they assume per home, then divide.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, civics

An open-fronted workshop with a glowing hearth, a great leather bellows, an anvil and tools on the wall.

  • A forge heats iron until it is soft enough to shape with a hammer.
  • Bellows blow extra air into the fire, which makes it burn much hotter.
  • Village smiths made and mended tools, hinges, nails and horseshoes.

Real size: About 20 feet wide. This model: Life size.

Try this: Which other things in your village need the smith? Stand by each one and find the iron in it. Teacher: Examples include the horse’s shoes, the well’s fittings, door hinges and farm tools.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, science, engineering

A small shop with a painted sign, a big brick oven inside and shelves of fresh loaves.

  • Bread rises because yeast gives off carbon dioxide gas, which makes bubbles in the dough.
  • A brick oven is heated with a fire, and the hot bricks keep on baking after the fire is raked out.
  • In many villages, families without an oven of their own paid to bake at a shared one.

Real size: About 20 feet wide. This model: Life size.

Try this: Follow a loaf backward. Which models does it pass through before it reaches this shelf? Teacher: Wheat plot, then windmill, then bakery. Students can add the granary for storage and the market stall for sale.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, science, economics

A tall stone tower mill whose four big sails turn in the wind, with a cap that can face them into it.

  • The turning sails drive heavy millstones inside, which grind grain into flour.
  • On a tower mill only the cap turns, so that the sails can face the wind.
  • Windmills were used to grind grain in Europe from the 1100s.

Real size: About 32 feet tall to the cap. This model: Life size.

Try this: Why build a windmill on high open ground, away from your barn and trees? Teacher: Tall things nearby block and disturb the wind, and open high ground catches it best.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, physics, engineering

A wooden stall under a striped awning, stacked with crates of apples, bread and vegetables.

  • A market is where people who make different things come together to trade.
  • Long before coins, people swapped goods, which is called bartering, and they also kept track of what they owed each other.
  • Many towns grew up around a place where a market was held regularly.

Real size: About 10 feet wide. This model: Life size.

Try this: Program it to call out what it sells with a say block. What would a farmer swap for a loaf of bread?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · economics, history, math

A round stone well under a little roof, with a windlass, a rope and a wooden bucket.

  • A well is dug deep enough to reach groundwater, the water held in the soil and rock below.
  • The stone lining stops the sides from falling in.
  • In 1854 Dr. John Snow traced a deadly cholera outbreak in London to one water pump. His work helped show that dirty water can spread disease.

Real size: About 5 feet across and 9 feet tall. This model: Life size.

Try this: Place this first. People carried water by hand, so how far would you want each home to be? Where should animals NOT be kept? Teacher: Homes should be a short walk away. Animals and waste should be kept well away, because they can pollute the water.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · science, history, health

A small timber grain store raised up on mushroom-shaped stones, with steps that stop short of the door.

  • Mushroom-shaped staddle stones lift a granary off the ground, and rats cannot easily climb past the overhang.
  • Air flowing underneath helps keep the grain dry so it does not rot.
  • Stored grain is what feeds a village through the winter and until the next harvest.

Real size: About 10 feet square. This model: Life size.

Try this: Why are the steps not joined to the door? What might climb them? Teacher: A gap in the steps stops rats and mice from walking straight up into the grain.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · history, science, engineering

A small arched plank bridge over a section of stream. Place more to make your stream longer.

  • An arched bridge pushes its load out along the curve and into the ground at each end.
  • Villages were often built by streams, for water and for power.
  • A shallow place where people could cross a river was often where a town began.

Real size: A 30-foot section of stream, with a 20-foot bridge. This model: Life size.

Try this: Press the green arrow to add more stream. What does your village get from a stream, and what might it do in a flood?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · engineering, geography, math

One 10-foot section of split-rail fence. Press its green arrow to lay three more in a straight line.

  • Fences keep animals in, and just as often keep them out of the crops.
  • Split rails were cut by driving wedges along the grain of a log.
  • Each section here is exactly 10 feet long.

Real size: Each section 10 feet long. This model: Life size.

Try this: A crop plot here is 20 feet on each side. How many sections does it take to fence one all the way round? How many for two plots side by side? Teacher: 8 sections for one plot (80 feet of perimeter). 12 for two side by side, since the shared side needs no fence between them (120 feet).

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · math, history

A black and white dairy cow, with a full udder, ready to graze wherever you put her.

  • A cow’s stomach has four compartments, which help it digest tough grass.
  • Cows chew cud, bringing food back up to chew it a second time.
  • A high-producing dairy cow can give several gallons of milk a day.

Real size: About 5 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: Life size, with the eyes drawn a little large.

Try this: Press the green arrow and watch her graze, then open her program and change one number. Can you keep her inside your fence?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, agriculture

A woolly sheep with a dark face and legs. Place a few together to make a flock.

  • Sheep were among the first animals people farmed, about 10,000 years ago.
  • Most wool sheep are sheared about once a year, and the wool grows back.
  • Sheep are flock animals, and tend to stay together for safety.

Real size: About 2.5 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: Life size, with the eyes drawn a little large.

Try this: What could your village make from wool? Which job would you need to add?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, agriculture, history

A sturdy pink and spotted farm pig with a round snout and curly tail.

  • Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud to keep cool.
  • Their strong snouts are made for digging up roots.
  • Pigs can eat kitchen scraps, which turned waste into food for a village.

Real size: About 2.5 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: Life size, with the eyes drawn a little large.

Try this: Pigs can eat scraps, so how close should they be to the houses? How close to the well?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, agriculture

A speckled hen with three small chicks at her feet, pecking around wherever you put them.

  • A hen can lay about one egg on most days when conditions are good.
  • A chick hatches after about 21 days of warming in the egg.
  • Hens scratch the ground and eat insects and seeds as well as grain.

Real size: A hen is about 1.5 feet tall. This model: Life size, with the eyes drawn a little large.

Try this: Press the green arrow, then change the numbers so they stay near the barn. How many eggs a week might three hens give? Teacher: About 15 to 18, if each hen lays on most days.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, agriculture

A huge, gentle work horse with feathered feet, wearing a padded collar and harness.

  • Draft horses are the largest horses, and many weigh around a ton.
  • A padded collar rests on the horse’s shoulders instead of its throat, so it can pull hard without choking.
  • Horse hoofs are protected by iron shoes, made and fitted by a smith.

Real size: About 6 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: Life size, with the eyes drawn a little large.

Try this: Press the green arrow and it walks up and down a field. Change the distance so it fits one of your plots. Teacher: A plot is 20 feet long, so the glide distance should be about 20.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, history, physics

A sure-footed brown and white goat with short horns, a beard and sideways pupils.

  • Goats were among the first animals people farmed, about 10,000 years ago.
  • They prefer to browse on leaves and shrubs rather than graze on grass.
  • A goat’s sideways pupils help it see a wide area around it.

Real size: About 2.5 feet tall at the shoulder. This model: Life size, with the eyes drawn a little large.

Try this: A goat can live where a cow cannot. Where in your village is the land too rough for crops?

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · biology, agriculture

A 20-foot square of ripe golden wheat. Press its green arrow to plant three more in a row.

  • Wheat was first farmed about 10,000 years ago in the Middle East.
  • The grains grow in a head at the top of each stalk, and are ground to make flour.
  • Wheat is planted each year, so seed has to be saved from one harvest for the next.

Real size: 20 feet on each side. This model: Life size.

Try this: How many plots will you plant? If each one feeds two people for a year, how many does your village need? Teacher: Answers depend on the village. The figure of two people per plot is a made-up rule for the activity, not a real yield.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · agriculture, biology, history, math

A 20-foot plot of corn, climbing beans and squash, grown together on low mounds.

  • Haudenosaunee and other Native American farmers have grown corn, beans and squash together for centuries.
  • The corn holds up the beans, and the broad squash leaves shade the soil and keep it moist.
  • Beans host bacteria on their roots that add nitrogen to the soil.

Real size: 20 feet on each side. This model: Life size.

Try this: Compare this with the Wheat Plot. Why might three plants grown together do better than one? Teacher: Each helps the others: support, nitrogen, shade and fewer weeds.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · agriculture, biology, history, world cultures

A 20-foot garden of neat rows, with cabbages, carrots, beans and a little wattle edging.

  • Different vegetables use different nutrients and attract different pests, so gardeners move them around each year. This is crop rotation.
  • Compost made from scraps and manure puts goodness back into the soil.
  • Carrots are roots, cabbages are leaves and beans are seeds, all parts of a plant we eat.

Real size: 20 feet on each side. This model: Life size.

Try this: Which animal would you keep near the garden for manure, and which would you fence out so it does not eat everything? Teacher: Answers vary. Manure from cows, horses or hens feeds the soil, while goats and pigs in particular must be kept out.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · agriculture, biology, health

A 20-foot flooded field with low earth banks and rows of green rice growing out of the water.

  • Rice feeds more than half of the people in the world.
  • Many rice farmers flood their fields, because rice can grow in standing water that drowns many weeds.
  • Low earth banks called bunds hold the water in.

Real size: 20 feet on each side. This model: Life size.

Try this: What does a rice field need that a wheat field does not? Where must it be in your village? Teacher: It needs plenty of water, so it belongs near a stream and on level ground.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · agriculture, geography, world cultures

A broad old apple tree with red fruit in its branches and windfalls in the grass.

  • Apples first came from the mountains of Central Asia, around what is now Kazakhstan.
  • An apple grown from a seed will not be like its parent, so growers copy good trees by grafting.
  • Bees carry pollen between apple blossoms so that fruit can form.

Real size: About 18 feet tall. This model: Life size, with the apples drawn a little large so you can see them.

Try this: Plant several to make an orchard, and think about what else you might add so the blossoms get pollinated. Search for the beehive.

Grades K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12 · agriculture, biology, history
